utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, may I ask the estimate of the time for the remainder of your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I would hope to finish at the end of tomorrow. To some degree dependent on the brevity or length of the answers of the witness, but come what may, I'll probably make decisions simply to bring matters to a conclusion. The longer his answers it may be the less topics we'll cover, but I'll do my best one way and another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice. Please continue with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I would like to tell you something important and very briefly. Several days ago Mr. Nice asked concrete evidence and proof about two things: That I spoke about Srebrenica, the crime in Srebrenica, earlier on, previously, and that previously I explained my attacks on Mr. Milosevic. I have brought all those concrete pieces of evidence. They are marked quotations, very brief, in these books, and I can hand over these books to the Tribunal if you so desire. I have them here in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, let both sides, both the Prosecution and the accused, have copies of your -- the documents which you say reinforce the evidence that you have given, and then they will decide how to use it. Do you understand? If the accused wishes to use it, then he can use it in re-examination. If Mr. Nice wishes to use it, he can use it in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, Mr. Robinson, your service should take this over. The quotations are all marked, and they should translate just those portions that have been highlighted in both these groups of books. Everything is highlighted. The quotations are very brief, and they can have it translated during the course of the day. I don't know how else we can get round this because I'm not in a position to be able to do that. If you order your service to take over the books straight away, then they can be placed at the disposal of both Mr. Nice and Mr. Milosevic in the course of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That would be very helpful. The sooner we have the photocopies, the sooner I'll be able to integrate questions about them with the questioning I planned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It's essentially for the parties to move on this, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in those circumstances, if he'd be good enough to make the books available to me, I'll get copies for myself and for the accused done probably within half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice. That's very helpful, yes. Yes. Would the court deputy please have the books passed over to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those four books, with the portions marked, explain the matter about the attack on Mr. Milosevic. The other three books have characteristic places where I speak about the crime in Srebrenica far before. So not to have them mixed up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we look at another extract from your interview from "The Death of Yugoslavia" programme. For the interpreters, we are at 25F. If we can play the tape, please, on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There it goes. No volume. No volume on this for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll start again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, start again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Milosevic helped Karadzic a great deal, without a doubt. And had it not been for Milosevic's aid who knows how it would all been with Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina. But many things in 1991 were slipping outside the control of Milosevic. He was always hesitating, hesitating to proclaim the nation, proclaiming autonomy of Serbian Krajina and so on. He was hesitant on the issue of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well, he was hesitant with regard to proclaiming a separate republic, blocked many other initiatives. And many he didn't succeed in stopping, blocking. At the same time, he provided assistance. He provided assistance continuously, that's a fact, and had it not been for Milosevic's help, who knows how all this would have appeared. Milosevic always made an effort to install his people in key positions in order to better control. He never liked Karadzic's nationalism, the renewal of Serb traditions, and so on. And he always tried to prevent that, thwart that."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you able to hear the text or the words?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is this a passage where you were telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's something that is overemphasised in this text and that is the personification aspect. When I say Milosevic assisted Karadzic, helped Karadzic, I'm talking about the Republic of Serbia and the authorities in the Republic of Serbia helping the authorities in Republika Srpska. So this kind of personification was customary in Serbian political life, and one should bear that in mind, and one should view that within the context in which it was uttered. So this type of personification was very widespread and customary, quite usual. But it is true that the authorities in Serbia, and indeed Mr. Milosevic, helped Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina, and every Serb helped as far as they were able. Anybody who refused was a traitor of the Serbs, there is no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then contained in this passage you say that the accused Milosevic was hesitating to proclaim the nation. Later on, at the end, you said that, "He never liked Karadzic's nationalism, the renewal of Serb traditions, and so on. He always tried to thwart that." What was it about Karadzic's nationalism that he apparently disliked?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm giving a general assessment here. Now, what Mr. Milosevic didn't like with respect to Mr. Karadzic, you'd have to ask Mr. Milosevic that first and foremost. These are my impressions. This is my position as an observer of their relationships. I can give you a characteristic example: Mr. Milosevic constantly advocated partisan traditions in political life in Serbia. Mr. Karadzic, on the other hand, was an advocate of Chetnik traditions, and it was on that basis that a civil war was waged in Yugoslavia amongst the Serbs themselves. During World War II, for example, two anti-fascist movements, they spent more energy fighting one another and their mutual conflicts than fighting the Germans and the German servants, lackeys. So those are the main dimensions which I talk about. However, specifically speaking, I couldn't tell you. I'm making a political assessment and evaluation. It is true that there was constant tension between Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Karadzic, for example; that's true too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you help me, Mr. Seselj, with what you mean by "partisan traditions."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's like this: In World War II, on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, there were in existence two anti-fascist movements, the partisan and the Chetnik movement. The partisan movement was under the leadership of the communists and the Chetnik movement was under the leadership and control of the emigres Yugoslav government which was in London, residing in London, and so this Chetnik movement was mostly made up of nationalists, whether Serb or Yugoslav nationalists, whereas the communists wished to take advantage of the struggle against the occupier to bring in a socialist revolution at the same time, and unfortunately, they succeeded in doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May that clip with the transcript be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 888.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, may I ask you, when you say that he never liked Karadzic's nationalism, you're not saying that he himself was not a nationalist but simply that he never liked the kind of nationalism that Karadzic exhibited?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. Robinson. What I'm saying here is this: I am implicitly stating that Mr. Milosevic was not a nationalist and he truly never was a nationalist, and Radovan Karadzic is a nationalist and that is why Radovan Karadzic was always politically closer to me than Mr. Milosevic. I'm very clear on that point. In the conflict between Milosevic and Karadzic, I was always on the side of Karadzic, although between myself and Karadzic there were some problems because Karadzic was politically closer in line to Kostunica, Djindjic, and the group of the old dissidents of the Belgrade intellectuals with whom I had certain frictions and even conflicts. So they are very complicated political relationships. We were never one political or ideological block; there were always internal strifes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the essence of the nationalism that both Karadzic and yourself supported?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the essence, the defence of Serb national interests. My nationalism was always deeper, more profound and better founded than Karadzic's nationalism, for example. You know, I was always more radical than Karadzic on many issues. However, our orientation was a nationalist one, nationalistic, which means the defence of Serb national interests, but I was in favour of the global project of a Greater Serbia whereas Mr. Karadzic was never in favour of a Greater Serbia. What he wanted was a community of Serb lands, for example, in which you would have Serbia, Montenegro, Republika Srpska, Republika Srpska Krajina, and at one point in time he transformed his own party into a Serb Democratic Party of the Serb lands, Serb territories.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I could have done that -- I could have accepted that as a minimum condition --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj, for the explanation. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll probably be turning comprehensively to the Greater Serbia issue tomorrow, if that helps. Could that last clip be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was. Sorry, I missed it. In which case, then let's move on to what for the interpreters will be 25H, and if the transcript of this video can be distributed. This is an amateur, I think, video. It's --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] It is the end of March, and the year is 1995. "Cheers. "Vojislav Seselj is addressing the Serbs from Glina rallied around, only four months before the Storm operation started. "Milosevic needed us both in 1991 and 1992. Besides, Slobodan Milosevic was helping the western Serbian countries at the time, Serbian Krajina as well as Republika Srpska. Serbian Krajina and Republika Srpska were established with his help. Besides that, he gave us, Radicals, weapons for 30.000 volunteers we were sending off to almost all the fronts where they were most needed. He also gave us buses, uniforms. He put the whole barracks in Bubanj Potok at the disposal of the Serbian Radical Party, for volunteers. We haven't forgotten that. And also in the first days after the battle in Borovo Selo, when we were transporting the weapons across the Danube to the Eastern Slavonia on rafts by night, that weaponry we got from the police warehouses and Serbian Territorial Defence warehouses pursuant to Milosevic's order. We returned Milosevic the favour. We supported him when he was having the toughest of times. "Plan Z-4, Zagreb-4. A humiliation for the Serbian people from the very beginning! What does Zagreb have to do with us the Serbs?! If this is a Z-4 plan, then it should be implemented in Zagreb! Let them tear and divide Zagreb instead! No plan can be accepted by the Serb side if it envisages integration of the Serbian Krajina into Croatia. Well, we, the Serbian Radicals, have sent 3.500 volunteers to the western Lika near Divoselo, Citluk and Pocitelj. "He will probably attack western Slavonia, if he decides to do so. Or perhaps Slunj, to merge with the 5th Corps, if the Serbs do not destroy the 5th Corps before that. But --"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can go right to the end but it may be helpful if we just pause it and then complete the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At this time, March 1995, your relationship with the accused was what; good, bad, or indifferent?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very hostile. On the 29th of January, 1995, I left the prison in Belgrade where I had spent four years. In March --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Months, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- there was a great tournament and tour of Srpska Krajina. I felt that there was a Croatian attack on Serbian Krajina being prepared. I had received certain information already that the Americans were involved and the American --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... your relationship. Now, if we look at the first part of the answer -- we'll come and look at the rest of it when we play the rest of it, but it's probably helpful to see it in parts. You give a number of facts about the accused helping Western Serbian countries at the time, giving you weapons for 30.000 volunteers. Was that accurate?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained that issue to you, who provided the volunteers and how the volunteers were sent. However, here I'm concentrating my attack on Mr. Milosevic himself and I am ascribing to him everything that was done by other levels of power and authority; the federal authorities, the JNA, over which he did not in fact have any control. So what I'm doing here is making an artificial -- painting an artificial picture which is black and white to make my attack on Milosevic as concentrated as possible, so I'm not mentioning Kadijevic, Adzic or anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're speaking to Serbs from Glina, and you're speaking about how you sent off your 30.000 volunteers heroically to the battlefield, and you're saying they were given their weapons by or on the order of the accused. How is that going to harm him?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it can do so in a very simplified black and white picture. It can compromise him politically because at that time I'm already feeling that there would be Croatian -- Croatian aggression and American help and the passive reaction. When Vance's plan was adopted for Serbian Krajina, Yugoslavia became duty-bound and took on the obligation in the case of a Croatian attack to militarily intervene to thwart that attack, and under those guarantees the Serbs from Krajina agreed to the Vance Plan. However, here we can feel, or they can feel that Croatia is getting ready to destroy Serbian Krajina with America's help. That's what they feel on the one hand, and on the other hand the passive approach to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Serbia towards that. And when Tudjman attacked Western Slavonia and then the Knin Krajina, Serbia did not intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This isn't addressed to your supporters, to loyal Serbs, and you're saying to them that Milosevic did everything he could to help, and you set it out in detail, and you say actually, "We returned Milosevic the favour, we supported him when he was having the toughest of times." The position is you were telling the truth on this, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite. I am waging a propaganda war against Mr. Milosevic here. Had he -- if really helped -- that he helped Republika Srpska Krajina, that is a fact because the federal authorities helped. But I'm -- what I'm doing here is carrying out a personification and ascribing to his person the actions of all the structures of power from Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and that's the whole point of this. That's the essence of the matter. So I stand by what I said and explained here, how the volunteers were sent out, how they were armed, and so on and so forth. I stand by that. But what I'm trying to do here is to overemphasise the attack on Milosevic and thereby to paint this black and white picture and that we helped him when he was in a very difficult position, that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So who was the even better friend of the Serbs who actually made the weaponry available, and why didn't you name that person? Who was it who had more power than the accused and was able to bring these things about?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kadijevic and Adzic were totally out of Mr. Milosevic's control. The volunteers went out within the JNA, but for me they were no longer important. Politically, they were totally insignificant for me at that time. Mr. Milosevic was then president of Serbia. A man from his party, Zoran Lilic, was president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The Croatian action against the Serb Krajina, with American assistance, was being prepared, so I am attacking Milosevic directly. This is a question of propaganda and political skills, not actually resorting to facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, help me with something. Where is the reference to the better friend?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, there's not a reference to the better friend. I have suggested to him that the friend of the Serbs is the accused as he's describing him, the man who armed them. He's saying it wasn't the accused, it was the other forces, so it's my question - the words don't appear there, I think - who is the better friend who actually did these services for you, and we've now had his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we play the rest of the tape, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not getting any translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] ... win back even what we did not manage to recover in 1991. And then to complete liberating everything that is ours --"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Press on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] -- Zadar, Karlobag, and finally to finish with Gospic because we have special motives for that, further on to liberate Karlovac where the majority of population has always been Serb, to liberate the entire Western Slavonia all the way to Virovitica. There is no other way. We can exchange territories, but always those of the same value. If Maslenica is so important to Tudjman, we will give it to him and he can give us the Dubrovnik coast stretch, let us say. That is the only the way in which we can exchange territories. We want -- we want the whole Pakrac. That is the only way clever politicians should negotiate territories. "Bothers and sisters Serbs. We, the Serbs, shall win. We cannot lose, we must not lose. What we manage to preserve as Serbian now, shall always remain Serbian. If we lose even a bit of our territories now, that will never be Serbian again. Serbian Krajina is not a part of Croatia. Serbian Krajina shall never be Croatian! "But, we should immediately move towards the first phase of unification, the direct and immediate unification of Republika Srpska and Serbian Krajina into a unique country, Western Serbia and Banja Luka as the capital. We must not allow to be torn apart and divided by others. Serbia will exist for as long as its children are loyal to her, may the Greater Serbia live!"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That passage, insofar as it contained facts, was it accurate? Not very many facts. It's mostly expressions of hope, but anything in it that you now disavow?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There is nothing I would disavow here except for one thing. At that time, I said that if we lose Serb territories, the Serb Krajina, it will never be Serb again. I said that by way of a warning. Although we have lost that temporarily and the Serb Krajina is under Croatian occupation nowadays, I'm convinced that some day it will be Serb again and that we are going to liberate all of Serb Krajina from Croatian Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. occupation. We will try to do so by peaceful means, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're concerned with what you were advancing in 1995. We see that you were speaking of the unification of Republika Srpska and Serbian Krajina into a unique country, and you go on to speak of Greater Serbia. Your intention that those should be linked and linked to Serbia? Was that your intention?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The intention was to link up the two wholes and set up an independent state that would be called Western Serbia. Further on in the future, there -- they could be united. I'm criticising the authorities of Serbia because they have an overly constructive attitude towards the Western powers. That is the thrust of my criticism. This was the position of the Serb Radical Party, uniting Republika Srpska and the Serb Krajina into a single state so that it would be easier to defend Serb territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On this tape, at least 90 or 95 per cent of the facts that you describe are accurate, and you say it's only the degree to which you emphasise the accused that needs to be reviewed or revised; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether the translation was faithful, but my speeches, inter alia, were directly aimed against Mr. Milosevic. I attacked his constructive attitude towards the Western powers. It would be necessary for you to play the entire speech here. Then everything would be clear. But you just get bits and pieces that you think support your own thesis and that is an improper way to proceed. Had you played the entire speech, everything would have been clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where in this speech do you say you attack Mr. Milosevic, or is it your contention that that attack is to be found somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice doesn't want to play that part of the speech to you. Mr. Nice doesn't want to play that part of the speech where I attack Mr. Milosevic. He selected only certain fragments that he believes may support his case, but he doesn't want to play the entire speech. If you were to hear the entire speech, then everything would be quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Leave it to Mr. Milosevic to bring that to our attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you remember what you said in the speech that was critical of Mr. Milosevic? Because this definitely is not, in my view. Your explanation doesn't give me any impression that this is critical of him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, I cannot recall each and every one of my speeches when I held hundreds of speeches. On this particular occasion, the Serb Krajina, I made at least 30 speeches. I started from Knin and I went all the way to Okucani. This was a tour going from one town to another, and I made speeches everywhere. Mr. Nice should play the entire speech. During those years, the end of 1993, and in 1994, and in 1995, and 1996, wherever I went I resorted to extreme propaganda and attacked Mr. Milosevic all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For my part may I make it clear that it's a totally unrealistic suggestion that every word of every speech made should be played when there are relevant parts in it on which it's quite appropriate to concentrate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this clip and transcript be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 889.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll now look at something different, an existing exhibit, which the interpreters will find at 25I and is Exhibit 643, tab 5. We're going back now to 1991, back in the chronology, to which the previous speech referred, but we're now back to a contemporaneous document. If you'd like to look at this document. It's not a very long document. And from the 1st Military District on the 18th of October, 1991, it comes from Major General Mile Babic. And it says so far as material, second paragraph -- if we can put it on the overhead projector. That's it. Bit further down the page. "During several consecutive contacts with Arkan, he stated that the weaponry, ammunition, mines and explosives had been supplied by the MUP of the interior and the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbia and that he'd been distributing them to Territorial Defence staffs in Erdut, Sarvas, Borovo Selo with records of the issued weapons being kept and updated." Now, you know about these things, about Arkan. You've told us a lot about him. Is this true?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do I know whether this is true or not? First of all, I don't know whether this is an original document or a forgery. I don't know who this General Mile Babic is. I never met that person. This has to do with the Serb Volunteer Guard of Zeljko Raznjatovic Arkan and I always kept my distance from him. As a matter of fact, we were engaged in a profound conflict. But you certainly have no documents to prove that the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party received weapons from the police. As for whether this is an original or a forgery, that is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The document's already been produced as an exhibit and its provenance and its genuineness has not been challenged. And you told us a great deal about your extensive knowledge of all these things. You know -- you know of no evidence, of no document, of nothing that would suggest this is incorrect where it shows the Ministry of the Interior, the Ministry of Defence supplying Arkan, do you? So it may be true.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Ministry of Defence certainly did not have any weapons or ammunition. I'm sure of that. Whether Arkan had some channels in the police or not can be the subject of a special investigation, but obviously an army general here probably engaged in security, because it says security organ of the 1st Military District. He is questioning Arkan, and he is presenting his own doubts. He is saying on the basis of several consecutive contacts with Arkan, Arkan stated that he received weapons from the police. Was Arkan telling the truth? Where is the proof that Arkan was speaking the truth? You would have to see in police warehouses whether he was actually given weapons. And you take for -- take it as a simple truth, the fact that Arkan stated this to Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The MUP and Ministry of Defence at that time would have been responsive to this accused Milosevic, and he would have thus, in my suggestion to you, have been responsible for the provision of these things to Arkan just as, in your interview, he was responsible for ensuring that you were armed. That's the truth and you know it, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not true. Arkan had such sophisticated weaponry that he certainly could not have got it from police warehouses. He obtained it from abroad for sure, because every one of his soldiers had a state of the art Heckler. That's not what the police had. That's not what the army had. Arkan did not get money from the police. And he was such a strong criminal and he was unchallenged. He never had a shortage of money. And there is one way in which he got money; he actually made prominent businessmen from Serbia pay up to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you heard the Judges ask, or His Honour Judge Robinson ask me earlier how long I'm going to be, and of course if you make very long answers where short ones will do, you will restrict the number of questions I can ask. If you'll take the opportunity to ask short questions [sic], we'll cover more ground. Now, just before I turn from this document, it may help you to know that it was provided by Serbia and Montenegro. You suggest it's a forgery, or may be. Do you have any reason to believe that Serbia and Montenegro has been providing this Court and this Office of the Prosecutor with forged documents?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the putsch of the 5th of October, a Mafia government was established in Serbia of Western mercenaries, and they started systematically persecuting all their political foes, especially Mr. Milosevic and his family. They persecuted his wife. They also brought criminal charges on the basis of trumped up charges. They persecuted his son and made him go abroad, and recently it was proven that they were a lie. Everything that the authorities did after the 5th of October 2002 against Mr. Milosevic was very dirty, very perfidious, and they resorted to all possible means. As for your fear that you're not going to finish my examination by tomorrow, well, you know, Mr. Nice, we haven't got anything in common there. As far as I'm concerned, I like it better in the courtroom than in a prison cell. I could go on coming until the New Year, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to invite the Court to be much firmer in restraining this witness from doing anything other than answer questions. We've spent so long in this Court listening to inappropriate observations, either from the accused or from witnesses, sometimes I become, or we all become, too tolerant. I would press the Court to restrict him simply to answering questions. The information I gave him was given neutrally and designed to assist him to abbreviate his answers, not to give him an opportunity to start making comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, as to forgery of documents, Mr. Seselj, please confine your answer, if you would be so good, as to help us with this: Do you know of any particular documents that you say the government, the more recent government, has forged in order to mislead this Court?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about any concrete ones, but at a press conference that was published in my book The Chetnik Vojvoda in Front of The Hague Tribunal, that is volume 51 of my collected works, I talk about a group of officers of the army of Yugoslavia who were given the task to forge official documents so that some things that were perhaps done by members of the military would be blamed on the police. Truth to tell, that had to do with Kosovo and Metohija, but if they were doing it in that sphere, they could have been doing it in this other sphere as well. About a month before I came to The Hague, or perhaps 15 days before I came to The Hague. The entire conference is published in my book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have the essence of your answer, which is that you have no evidence of any particular documents that you say the more recent government has forged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Safe to say, Your Honour, and I'm grateful to the witness for saying this:

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You tell us, Mr. Seselj, that there was a group of officers of the army given the task to forge official documents. Is that the VJ commission that prepared material in relation to events in Kosovo after -- after March 1999? Is that the body that was aimed to forge documents?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I cannot say that. Now you are trying to generalise my statement, the one I made at the press conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us move on. We have the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have to say I'm interested in this because -- because it's been a feature of earlier evidence and it has a bearing on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let us hear you, Mr. Seselj, on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With Your Honours' leave:

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not a point of generalising it, Mr,. Seselj. I'd like you to particularise it. You've told us about a group of army officers and we've heard about a group of army officers that included, for example, General Gojovic, and General Delic was engaged in it, and various others, and they had a big organisation to put together material in 2000 to cover events in Kosovo. Now, this is the only group we've heard of. Is this the group that you know was forging documents?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At this press conference I mentioned the names of some officers, but their ranks were up to the rank of colonel. That can be seen in my book The Chetnik Vojvoda Before The Hague Tribunal. This was after the 5th of October, after some police generals were removed. And some police generals did take part in the putsch of the 5th of October, 2000. Among some of the army generals, there was some fear. They were afraid that they would be indicted before The Hague Tribunal, et cetera, and some things that they thought might be relevant for indictments they ascribed to the police, and that's what I said at that press conference of mine. If you wish to see that, you can. It's available. But now to speculate any further on the basis of one statement, that is impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've been able to locate various volumes already today. You've been able to identify this particular volume. Do you have it in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it here in The Hague but I didn't look for it. Mr. Bonomy, I can bring it in already tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be helpful if you were able to identify the passage that relates to this for tomorrow, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let me turn to something a little different -- oh, no, just before we do and in case you don't find the extract, can you give us an example of the deceit that these officers practised; i.e., what was it they made up, how was it they changed history? Can you give us an example?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again you're generalising. What do you mean that they were forging history? If the members of the military were responsible for a particular act, they were trying to blame the police for it. As for General Delic, I don't think that he participated in any such thing. He is a very brave and courageous person and officer, an honourable man, and I don't think that he would have anything to do with any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It would help me, though, Mr. Seselj, if you were able to give an example of an incident which -- for which responsibility was transferred from the army to the police.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're expecting me to be omnipotent. From the 5th of October onwards I was an opposition person, and I was in constant clash with the new pro-Western regime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have accused Mr. Nice a number of times this morning of generalising. Now, what is it you're doing other than generalising if you make such a sweeping statement and can't give an example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can show you the contents of my press conference from the beginning of 2001, and I can give you other examples, but as a politician in political life you bet I can generalise, and I did generalise so many things. Mr. Nice is not a politician here. He is a prosecutor, an international prosecutor, at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think it would be wrong to let that go. You're not here either as a politician. You're here as a witness dealing with matters of relevant interest in relation to grave accusations and it would be useful if you did not use the arena for political grandstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look at another exhibit which is an excerpt from a book. It's, for the interpreters, 27. We provided a much larger Serbian text for context and re-examination if any. It was just one passage that I want to explore with the witness. The book, I think, was published in January 1992, and is headed "Politics as a Conscientious Challenge," and Mr. Seselj, if you've got the marked passage, which I hope you have, there is this extract which you can explain for us. You said: "As for Milan Babic --" English on the overhead projector, please. Just the first page, Mr. Nort, will do, I think. I'll find it. It begins "As for Milan Babic ..." Sorry it isn't marked. 145, page number, Mr. Seselj. I'm sorry that wasn't marked in advance. It has you saying this, that: "As for Milan Babic, we do not have a special alliance - we are personal friends, but Milan Martic is also a personal friend of mine, and I never gave priority to one over the other, and I was deeply affected, deeply hurt when I found out that they were in discord ..." First of all, is that a correct reflection of your position in January 1992?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That reflects my position from January 1992. I considered Milan Babic and Milan Martic to be my personal friends. I was very sorry that they were in a latent conflict, and several times I tried to bring about a reconciliation between the two. In the meantime, I've changed my mind about Milan Babic and now I consider him to be a thoroughly dishonest and dishonourable person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've heard about that and we may come back to it. The next little passage we've got, though, comes from the mouth of Captain Dragan where he says this: "The Chetniks of Vojvoda Seselj - I do not know if that is the right wording. They were young men who decided to join the resistance through the Serbian Radical Party." This is on page 146. I'm grateful. "I had several of them in my units and they proved themselves to be exceptional soldiers, absolutely loyal. Several of these young men participated in the battle for Banija, which was certainly a decisive battle led by Special Units of the Krajina MUP, which were under my command at the time." Is Dragan right in saying that your Chetniks served under him? It's in your book, you see.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: A number, I don't know exactly how many, went to his training centre. Captain Dragan, however, is lying when he says he was in command of the battle for Banija. He was never in command of any combat unit nor was he ever in a place where there was shooting and where he could get killed. He is simply boasting here, exaggerating his role in the war. According to what I know, he never saw combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This was published in a book where you both participated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 890.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not correct, Mr. Nice. The book contains our interview for the Duga newspaper on page 149. This was done by journalist Liljana Habjanovic Djurovic, and it was published in the Duga of the 4th of January, 1992. She interviewed both of us and then compared our responses to the same questions. It wasn't I who introduced Captain Dragan into my book. I simply transmitted in my book this interview published in Duga where our responses were put together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look at the next exhibit, which is another book extract dealing with your relationship, number 28, dealing again with Babic and with Dragan. This is a book of yours, when it comes to you. It's your book "Current Political Challenges" published in October -- well, Belgrade 1993, I think. And if you'd go, please, to the short passage that's been highlighted with the figures 1 to 5. You said these things, and we'll just look at them quite quickly. If the usher can get the English version on the overhead projector. You said: "I went three times to help Milan Babic. I went when Jovan Raskovic tried to bring him down." It says that you had gone to a fervent rally in Knin where they tried to bring Babic down by force. You went when Dragan went to brim him down, calling his soldiers from the front to bring Babic down, and you clashed with Dragan. And you said: "As long as I thought that Babic was acting in the interest of the Serbian people and for the benefit of the Serbian cause, I always unreservedly supported him. "... I consider Babic to be an intelligent man and a talented politician. And I am sorry that the Serbian Krajina lost ..." him. Now, you've said some very bad things about Mr. Babic while you've been here. Just, please, point, so we can understand it, to why it is you've changed your mind. Just summarise it shortly.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is correct that I went to Knin on several occasions, and what it says about the conflict between Babic and Raskovic, Babic and Martic, Babic and Captain Dragan and so on. However, Milan Babic has proved to be a dishonourable man. After the elections in 1993 and in early 1994, we formed a coalition. We were supposed to have a coalition government of -- because that was the third largest party, our party, and Babic's was the strongest party, and we signed an agreement in Belgrade, in the press Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. centre, that he would be the Prime Minister, and we distributed all the ministerial portfolios and then he simply trampled on our agreement without consulting us, and he entered into a coalition with Borislav Mikelic. And in our view, he lost all honour and honesty. We had no further respect for him. And then Milan Babic turned up here as a man who entered into a plea agreement with the OTP and agreed to testify falsely against others in order to have his sentence reduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His evidence is going to be weighed by the Judges, you see, not by you. And you've been expansive in an account of your own courage and bravery. Do you understand, Mr. Seselj, that Mr. Babic came and gave evidence against his interest, knowing that he would be imprisoned and separated from his family. Do you regard that as an act of courage in a man if he's telling the truth? Tell us.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You tricked Milan Babic. You promised him that maybe he would not be indicted if he testified falsely against Mr. Milosevic and some other people, and when he did that dirty job then you arrested him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and I'm going to ask you, please, since you choose to use a word like that, "tricked," without getting excited, just give us the evidence upon which you rely for that assertion. And if you have none, would you be good enough to say so.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have evidence. You interviewed Milan Babic more than once. You told him he was a suspect and that it was possible that an indictment would be raised against him. You offered him cooperation. In fear of an indictment, he agreed to testify falsely against Mr. Milosevic. After he had done this dirty job, he was indicted anyway. You can ask him now whether he's disappointed or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're being asked for the evidence for this assertion. You're not being asked to just repeat the assertion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The evidence is in the transcripts of the interviews of Mr. Milan Babic. Mr. Nice asked me why I had changed my attitude towards Milan Babic. I explained this. Now you're asking me to provide evidence. Why would I need evidence to change my position, evidence on paper?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a perversion of what's actually taking place here at the moment, with all due respect to you. You're simply being asked to state what the evidence is on which you claim that the Prosecution tricked him, and so far you haven't identified any. And if you haven't any to identify, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll move on, and perhaps we can have this exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let it be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 891.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just to -- Mr. Nort.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just so that we can follow a little bit more of your relationship with these parties and in particular with Captain Dragan, we'll play another short clip when the transcript has been distributed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters have a reference, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. Yes. It's 28A. I'm going to try -- for your assistance, I'm going mostly straight through the list, but -- for their assistance. I beg your pardon. I shouldn't talk to them directly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] During the inspection of combat position, Captain Dragan came. Let's see what it looked like when they met. "What joint combat? We sent a dispatch to the President ... "And where is he located? "No, he's not there. He went over there. "The first day of the combat, Monday, the first day of the combat, what happened then? "And where is he located? "No, he is not there, no, no, no. He went over there. Uzelac. Where is the guy with the -- "No, he's there. "Captain Dragan objected because he was against the Chetniks. "Commander, come here. We won't argue. "No, but you agree that I would not -- "For him Babic is the hero. I'm just a workout instructor. "You got us involved in politics, and you shouldn't have. "If the truth is not useful in wartime, you must not say it. "Well, you must have made a conclusion yourself. "I did make a conclusion. "There are other battlefields for Captain Dragan in Western Slavonia. They yearn for experienced commanders over there. There are also battlefields in Eastern Slavonia and elsewhere. "But the captain came here first. "Well, he came here, and he has done a lot here ... "Listen, you have Milan Babic here. He's your hero. "Listen, you must not put it that way. "You declared him a hero. "Today you are turning the army against the Krajina Prime Minister. "He is a coward and a betrayer who has broken up our unit, who has broken up Knin. "You are the one who is breaking it up, you are breaking the battlefield right here, and you should not have come to inspect ... You are the one who is breaking the battlefield. It must not be done. "Please, since this is my territory, I would --"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please just pause it there. Do you remember this exchange with Dragan about Babic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned this conversation a few days ago. This is a tape shot on the first front line near Benkovac where I was visiting the Serb positions. Captain Dragan suddenly turned up, evidently wishing to meet me. That was my visit to Knin in November 1991 when I was invited by Milan Babic to save him from Captain Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it clear that you were entirely on the side of Babic at this time, although you go on to say you came to make peace between Babic and Martic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you were opposed to what the man Dragan was doing?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Captain Dragan tried to get the army to rebel at the front lines, and he was going to have a rally against Babic in Knin, attempting to carry out a coup d'etat. I gave two interviews on the radio, one on the state radio of Knin and the other on the youth radio of Knin, and I spoke very sharply against Captain Dragan, because even after our meeting at Benkovac, he continued doing what he was doing. I think that my interviews on those two radio stations were key in preventing Captain Dragan from carrying out his coup d'etat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, to save time, the rest of the transcript is available. If it can be produced in full, it's only another couple of slides but every side saves time. If that can be done, and I'll put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the material we've looked at just recently, the truth is that you were against Babic in this Court, whatever may have been the political history after 1993, but you're against Babic in this Court simply because he's given evidence against this accused, aren't you, and contemporaneous material gives a more accurate picture of your judgement of him at the time.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. I definitely turned against Milan Babic in 1994 when he unilaterally trampled on our coalition agreement. After that, we never met again until 2003 when he turned up here in the Detention Unit of The Hague Tribunal. We had no contact before his testimony against Milosevic. That is not correct. My attitude towards him was negative from before, but of course his false testimony against Mr. Milosevic is an additional reason for my negative attitude towards him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May this then be exhibited, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 892.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This comes -- this comes from your book "The Chief of the General Staff on His Knees," tab 29 for the interpreters. Yes, it's on page 172, Mr. Seselj. If you'd be good enough to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: More pages provided for context and examination and so on but I don't need to ask him very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In this book of yours published in 1993, you said this when asked if Martic had rejected volunteers in Krajina. You said: "He never -- Milan Martic never rejected the help of volunteers in the Serbian Krajina!" A journalist said that he, the journalist, was in Knin when Martic stated on television that fighters from other theatres of war had been contacting him and the army had refused to take them on. And you said: "Please, we were in coordination with Martic during the attack on Krajina. In agreement with the Main Staff and General Mile Novakovic and Milan Martic, the minister of the interior, we sent 3.200 volunteers between three to four days and there had never been any problems with our volunteers and never had Milan Martic stated that our volunteers hadn't gone there -- needn't have gone there." I'm grateful. And then: "As for crimes, Milan Martic had never --" later on about Leskovac. "As for crimes, Milan Martic has never been engaged in criminal activities and I would not connect him to this." And you said that he had a conflict with Arkan that shouldn't be confused with his relationship with volunteers. But back to the first larger answer, is it right that you sent 3.200 volunteers within three to four days?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that here a few days ago and that we did this in agreement with the representative office of the Republika Srpska Krajina in Belgrade, and I confirmed that here, that this was done in agreement with Milan Martic and General Mile Novakovic. And that's what you said Mr. Milosevic was doing based on some statements, but this is what actually happened. This is correct. When the Croats attacked Citluk, Divoselo, and some other Serb villages, we sent 3.500 volunteers there. They arrived there and were deployed there, but then through a diplomatic initiative the Croats halted their attack and that's why they never participated in the fighting. I was trying to explain this here the other day. Thank you, Mr. Nice, for corroborating the truth of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are various accounts on things sometimes before the Court because in due course it may be the Court will be able to decide where the truth lies including from your statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May this one be exhibited, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's only one English page in this but there are several --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Provided for some greater context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So should exhibition be confined just to the Serb -- the relative Serb part along with the English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm in the Court's hands. The witness has occasionally complained about lack of context and so we've sometimes produced rather more pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's do the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now let's look at something --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Nice. That will be Exhibit 893.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Number 30, please, for the interpreters. Maybe here there may be a few more passages to look at than have been marked, Mr. Seselj, but I see that there are one or two things that I wanted to raise with you again this morning. So that may take just a second or so to find.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing is marked in my copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First of all, if I can find it, in the English -- this is a speech you made on the 11th of November of 1993. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the Court will be good enough to go to the second page in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the title of the book?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The title of the book is "The General on His Knees," I think. "The Chief of the General Staff on His Knees." If the Court would go to the end of the second page and to the end of the very long paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if you, Mr. Seselj, would go, please, to what I think will be page 288, roughly in the middle, at the end of a paragraph, we find you're saying this to the audience when you're complaining about various bad things that have been done by way of forgery, and you then say this, three-quarters of the way down: "It's the best proof of what kind of forgeries the police use, and the best proof of our claim that the police have a great deal of control over some state organs -- state organs in the Republic of Serbian Krajina and their Bureau in Belgrade." Then this: "You already know what they do in Eastern Slavonia and Baranja. The Red Berets operate as a paramilitary formation of the Serbian State Security Service under the command of Mihalj Kertes and Franko Simatovic called Frenki and some other people from the Serbian Ministry of the Interior." You know what I'm going to ask you, Mr. Seselj, don't you. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a press conference that I held in the headquarters of the Serb Radical Party sometime in November. This is the 11th of November, 1993, after Ljubisa Petkovic, the vice-president of the Serb Radical Party, had been unmasked as an agent of the state security whose aim was to break up the party. In his possession, we found a vehicle and a traffic licence. The police allowed him to use its vehicle. I kept Ljubisa Petkovic in my office and invited two television crews, Politika and Studio B, and interviewed him about this. And now I'm telling the journalists what happened - this is the bit that you skipped here because you're not interested in it - and then I am attacking the state security service which is trying to destroy our party. And at the end I say that the police tried to assassinate me, because there had been a traffic accident and I, as the head of a group of deputies, was in a vehicle driving along Knez Mihailo Street in front of the American embassy in Belgrade -- you don't want to hear my response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you're not answering the question. The way this system works is you're supposed to answer the questions you're asked, not tell us what you want to tell us. And the question was very simple: Is the statement true or not? Why can't you deal with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But my response cannot be complete if I don't give you the context. You're avoiding the context. I am here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why don't you start by telling us whether it is true or not and then add any explanation you feel is necessary. Is that not a better way to do it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because, Mr. Bonomy, I have learned through these ten days that if I give you that kind of answer, you'll interrupt me and say thank you, you've answered the question. However, an incomplete response is not a true response, and it can be misused to support something that is quite the opposite of what I'm testifying to here. Here I am attacking the state security service by all means, because I have discovered that my closest associate was an agent of theirs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I simply note that you have not answered the question in spite of being given every opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, the documents -- the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have replied.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- documents have been provided for you, for the accused, and for the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, let's be clear about this. You gave an explanation. You put the matter in context. What do you say now as to the question which was put regarding the last sentence in that paragraph, the Red Berets operate as a paramilitary formation of the Serbian State Security Service under the command of Kertes and Frenki and some other people from the Serbian Ministry of the Interior. We have allowed you to give your explanation to put it in context, but what is the answer to the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here I am constructing an artificial institutional link between the fact that this unit, the Red Berets, existed in Srpska Krajina, that for a time it was commanded by Frenki, and that Frenki was a high-ranking official of the State Security Service of Serbia. I'm constructing this in order to strengthen my attack. This is evident. There was no institutional link, but I constructed one, because I wanted to strike the strongest possible blow against the SDB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, you and the accused and other witnesses for the accused are saying that the Red Berets didn't come into being until 1996, and here you are in 1993 giving an account voluntarily at a press conference in your own political hall that completely matches the evidence from the video of the Prosecution. What you said here is true, isn't it? Let's just break it down into two parts: The Red Berets were a paramilitary formation, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Red Berets were not a paramilitary organisation. The Red Berets in Serbian Krajina were a special unit of the police of Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In 1992, 1991, when? This --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1991 until the fall of Srpska Krajina, there was a unit of the police of Srpska Krajina which was popularly referred to by the people as the Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By the police or by the Serbian State Security Service? Do you mean the Serbian State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a unit of the police of Srpska Krajina, and I am attributing that unit to the SDB. And during those years it wasn't only I myself who did that. People from other opposition parties did that, from the so-called non-governmental organisations and pro-Western media. Quite simply, that kind of mood prevailed. It's your problem that you wrote an indictment based on our public statements and not on the basis of documents and facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, in a lot of your interviews at the time, as we can see, you were alert to the illegality and problems of paramilitary units because you were always saying that your men were not paramilitary units. You'll see that later. And here you are making a positive assertion that the Red Berets were paramilitary. That's because they were. They were a straight, unlawful, paramilitary group created by this accused, disturbing the peace of the former Yugoslavia, and you knew that.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not true. The Red Berets were never a paramilitary organisation. I know full well what a paramilitary organisation means. It's always in a negative context. And here, when I wish to insult somebody, I call them a paramilitary formation, because that's a very strong insult, which means criminality, war crimes, and a whole lot of other things to boot within that concept.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally on this passage, the group that existed between 1991 and 1993 when you made this statement at a press conference had been headed by Frenki Simatovic, as you said.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure that throughout that time he was at the head, but he was a volunteer in the police of Republika Srpska Krajina, and he was in charge of intelligence, and at one point in time he was head of a unit, but I couldn't tell you from what date to what date, but it's no secret that he was there as a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So the things we saw on the video of the ceremony at Kula camp being said by Simatovic begin to look as though they were true, don't they?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the video we saw Simatovic proud of his participation in the war, him and his combatants. And the traditions of his participation in the war he links up with a unit that was formed in 1996, because everybody wants to have certain traditions to which to refer to, some glorious past. But formally speaking, institutionally speaking, the unit was a component part of the SDB and formed in 1996. It was not institutionally within the service of the State Security Service of Serbia before that, and you have Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. no evidence or proof to show the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, the last part of your answer about whether evidence exists is not for you to say, and typically it wouldn't lead to another question from me, but since you make that point, just help us: The video that we've seen, which is evidence of what Simatovic said and of the accused standing there, listening to every word and reviewing the officers, and Stanisic speaking, do you want to say in some way that that's a forgery or construction since you say we have no evidence? Do you?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe -- or, rather, I can't say whether it's a forgery or not, but that's no evidence. Frenki is referring to his own war past, which he considers to be glorious, as he does his combatants, and that's the only conclusion I can draw from that particular video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, let's be clear about this. The last sentence, you say, is a misdescription of the Red Berets. You have mischaracterised them as a paramilitary formation of the state security, Serbian state security, and you did that deliberately because you wanted to insult, you say, the Serbian Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. I did it intentionally, deliberately, to strike a blow against the security service, because from this entire text, over several pages, you can see how profound and deep the conflict was. In a political sense, they were after my head. They were trying to destroy the Serbian Radical Party by various secret, clandestine police means. And my response is brutal. You couldn't have a more brutal response, and at the end of the text I even accuse them of trying to assassinate me. And the fact that there was really an accident, that there was a police car in front of me which turned unlawfully and that my driver crashed into it, and I did injure my head and had some blood going down my face and head in front of the American embassy, which was slightly demeaning for me, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So at the time you were in conflict with the Serbian Ministry of the Interior, they were after you, and this is the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- explanation for this mischaracterisation of the Red Berets as a paramilitary formation of the Serbian State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I wanted to insult them. I wanted to inflict a blow. I wanted to have a reaction from them and to make then generally mad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We are past the time for the break. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, may we just clarify one issue. Mr. Seselj brought in seven of his books because Mr. Nice asked him to do so or, rather, he asked to see evidence about the fact that Mr. Seselj had previously spoken about certain matters, the attacks on me, Srebrenica, and so on and so forth. You said that the parties should be supplied with these documents so that we see who is going to ask what, but I don't think that should be at the expense of my time. Mr. Nice sought this evidence, so it is his duty to spend his time to ask questions, because I am not challenging Mr. Seselj's testimony here, it is Mr. Nice who is challenging it. He asked for evidence, he received evidence, so he can ask the questions. Now, if I have to use my time for re-examination on this, then that would be improper as far as the proper use of my time is concerned. I have now received these photocopies of the seven books.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, do you intend to follow up on this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, when I've read them I may indeed follow up on it, but the accused's point is entirely misconceived. Where witnesses -- sorry, nothing else. I may follow up on it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just let me know, because I have an interest in seeing what is in the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We will probably have reviewed them by the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But more probably tomorrow will be the time I will deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we stay with the same document, which is the extract from The Chief of the General Staff on His Knees, and Mr. Seselj, would you please go on now to what is in English page 5, and what is marked in your version. It's to be found on page 290. We see -- we see halfway down the page quite a long passage which I must read to you and then ask you some questions about it. It reads as follows. I'm going to start just above the markings on the photocopy: "What the public didn't know --" further up. Above that, please. "What the public did not know is that our volunteers also fought with special police units from Serbia and the Yugoslav army, which would cross the Drina and Danube from Serbia and take part in fights." Just pausing there, is that sentence true?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you would have to read that entire portion, Mr. Nice. It's not that simple. If you don't want to read it, I'll read it, with the Court's indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, it's a very simple question. I'm going to ask it once more. If you can't answer it shortly, we're going to move on. Do your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I think to be fair to the witness he has to be allowed to put it in context. He is saying it's not a question that admits of a simple yes or no, and that is so in some cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, a witness can always say that, but in this case the question to which I would be grateful for an answer is a simple one at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did volunteers fight with special police units from Serbia and the Yugoslav army which crossed the Drina and Danube from Serbia and took part in fights? It seems to me a very simple question, if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I say here is that volunteers fought in the units of the former JNA, the Territorial Defence, the army of Republika Srpska Krajina, and the -- those two republics. And then, wishing to attack, I go on to speak about the special police units and -- and army units, and I highlight Frenki, and I overemphasise the conclusion on the basis of the fact that Frenki --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is this sentence -- I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I -- just before you do that, though, what I think Mr. Seselj is drawing attention to is the immediately preceding passage which says, "Everybody knew that our volunteers fought within..." and then it says, "the units of the Yugoslav People's Army, the Territorial Defence of the Serbian Army of Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina," and then it goes on to say, "as well as within the Serbian police of these two Serbian republics." And then it contrasts that knowledge with, "What the public did not know is that our volunteers also fought ..." Now, you say, if I'm understanding you correctly, Mr. Seselj, that that is an entirely inaccurate statement, what follows.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What follows is my attack on the state security service within that same context here, and you can see that a large number of pages, in actual fact, is devoted to that attack, and I combine truthful facts and my imagination and through that combination I'm telling my sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, what I have difficulty with here is that you're contrasting what everybody knows with something of which you claim intimate knowledge and you're therefore likely to mislead your audience, are you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's like this: In a political struggle and in a propaganda campaign, sometimes your goal is to inflict damage on the enemy by partially misleading the public with respect to certain facts. That is a legal propaganda tool in political settling of accounts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Without beating about the bush, you lied to the public in order to achieve political end. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You're lying to the public. I waged a propaganda war against Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, we have spoken about this on many occasions. You are not to characterise the Prosecutor as lying. We have been through that before. He's putting his case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, on the basis that this sentence is therefore untrue, let's read on the next sentence, shall we, follow it through? "Mr. Vakic, the Serbian Radical Party member, is here. He is also a prominent member -- commander of our volunteers, who received the following letter of thanks from the Serbian Ministry of the Interior Special Purposes Unit: 'To the commander of the Old Serbia Volunteer Detachment, the Duke Branislav Vakic from Nis for the successful operation during the fight for the freedom of the Serbs in Republika Srpska.' This was issued in Bajina Basta on the 25th of May, 1993, after the fight near Skelani. It was signed by Franko Simatovic, also known as Frenki. He is presently the head of the Serbian State Security Service Intelligence Administration. This is the original document." So may we take it that you were standing there, waving a piece of paper at your audience? Is that what you were doing?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was at a press conference. The document is not an original one. There was some document which was brought in by Branislav Vakic when the volunteers returned from the front. Then they handed over to the border authorities of the police a certain quantity of weapons which they did not return. And that is the only fact here. All the rest is speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pause. The document, because we've only got sort of your account here at the moment in this book. When you address the people, ladies and gentlemen, treating them in a respectful way, and you tell them, you say, "Mr. Vakic is here, a prominent commander of our volunteers," and you read out the letter of thanks from Frenki, well, showing that they were subordinated to and working for Frenki. Did Vakic resist your giving this description of events?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all that, does not mean that they were subordinated to Frenki, and they weren't subordinated to Frenki. Secondly, Vakic did have some piece of paper to which was attached some kind of memorandum. I can't remember exactly what that piece of paper was, but it served a useful purpose for us at the press conference within the context of everything that we presented against the State Security Service of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, at -- can I take it that it was an accurate statement at that time that Frenki was in office as the head of the Serbian State Security Service Intelligence Administration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was -- I say here today he is head of the Intelligence Administration of the State Security Service, and that is the 11th of November, 1993, that we are talking about. So according to my information then, he was at that time the head of the intelligence department. What he was before that I can't say for sure. And so I'm attacking him at that point in time, assuming that as head of the Intelligence Administration he was one of the main men in the secret propaganda war against the Serbian Radical Party. And I assume that he launched that drive, and I'm trying to do him as much harm as possible by inflicting counter-blows, and that's the only truth in all this. Now, perhaps Mr. Nice doesn't like the methods that I used to do that. That's another matter entirely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The difficulty for me again is trying to understand how this is a counter-blow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, let's just deal with the document, the piece of paper that you read from, quoted from. I'm afraid I haven't had this prepared in enough numbers, it can be done in due course, but perhaps the usher can put -- yes, they will be done in a second, but perhaps we can put that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, would you like me to answer that question of yours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'd like to hear the answer. How is it a counter-blow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
