utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, it's the end of 1993 we're talking about here, when the state security service en masse was arresting volunteers belonging to the Serbian Radical Party and issuing public statements, statements for the public showing on television enormous stockpiles of weapons, and the thesis they are promoting is that that was seized from the volunteers arrested. We are being accused of different things; war crimes, looting, crimes of different types and general madness. There is nothing that they didn't ascribe to us. And I am returning that, and I am saying to the police now you're seizing the weapons that you provided them with. So I am defending myself and defending the party from annihilation. And what happened later on? One month later all those volunteers, once the pre-election campaign was over, were released. No -- none of them were sentenced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But, I mean, forgive me for having read on a little in this, but the theme of this is for you to explain is that the Serb Radical Party volunteers were acting with official approval. That's what this is about as I read it. Now, that aligns you with the government, and I have difficulty understanding how this is a put-down of the government.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, the volunteers went to war as soldiers of the JNA. After recognition of independence of Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the 6th of April, they stayed in the JNA until the 19th of May. After the 19th of May, they did not go through the JNA any more, via the JNA, they went by reporting individually and joined up with the army of Republika Srpska. Some even joined the police of Republika Srpska and other people did this in groups. They would make contact and leave. So this was no longer with the approval of the authorities in Belgrade, or their permission, but the authorities could not stop this process because they didn't cross the Drina River with weapons, they crossed as civilians and joined up in the military formations once they were over the river. So that's it. And that was the time when we were in conflict over the Vance-Owen Plan. Mr. Milosevic, for instance, was demonstrating a high degree of cooperativeness with the Western powers with respect to that plan whereas I am trying to thwart that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean, then, that when you say, "We were acting through the formal organs of the Serb government," that that's an inaccurate statement for the period after May 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that way, I wish to create additional problems for Mr. Milosevic, to force him to explain to his diplomats, the ones he contacted from the West, to explain this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Also, Mr. Seselj, you would ascribe the same significance to the statement, "This is meant for you to say that the volunteers went to fight completely officially." Is that true or false? That's the next line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the 19th of May, 1992, they went officially within the composition of the JNA. Or rather, after the 19th of May --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Before the 19th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and then after the 19th individuals went unofficially as civilians to Republika Srpska and joined up to the army of Republika Srpska there then. That's what I want to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, just -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's just look at the document that you've described as some sort of document because you published it in your magazine, and it's on the overhead projector at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if the booth could focus on the -- if the booth could focus the screen on the picture or the document there. Can it be enlarged? Can you now enlarge, magnify it? Thank you. More, more, more, more, more. That will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is the document you were reading from, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look at the stamp at the bottom. Why is --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the stamp cut off here?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's your magazine, you tell us. But this is the document you were quoting from, and you published it in your magazine. Come along, read it out for us, will you?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I haven't got it in full here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you read out what's on the screen, please, for us.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, why don't you read it out, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not for you to ask questions. It's not for you to run the evidence. This is a document from your magazine --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, may I have the entire document for me to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You may in due course, but at the moment I'm asking you to read something from your magazine on the screen. Will you do so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just read what is on the front page, Mr. Seselj. Interpreters --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You must provide me with the entire document for me to be able to read the heading and everything else. Then I will give you it in full. What is this, hide and seek? I'm sure there is something in the title that Mr. Nice likes very much, and then I'll be able to explain how it came about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you don't determine how the evidence is managed in the case. The Prosecutor has asked you a question. He has asked you to read it. Are you saying you're not going to read it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Somebody -- well, I'd like to draw your attention to what it says. It says: "Is giving --" The Ijekavian dialect is used. That is very important. "Dodjeljuje," "Is bestowing a certificate of gratitude to Vojvoda Vakic Branislav for his success," and the "success" is in the Ijekavian dialect as well, I-J, "and cooperation during combat in the struggle for the freedom of the Serb people in Republika Srpska. Bajina Basta, the 25th of May."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Signed apparently by?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you see who signed it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whose signature that is. Quite possibly it's Frenki's but I'm not quite sure. How should I know what his signature looks like?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is this the document that you read out to your audience on that day in November 1993, and you then published it in your magazine, on each occasion presenting it as genuine, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I presented it as an authentic document, but now I assert that it is not an authentic document and that its original doesn't exist, because had this been an authentic document of the SDB of Serbia, it would not have said "dodjeljuje" in the Ijekavian, and it wouldn't have said "uspjehe," again in the Ijekavian. It is impossible for the State Security Service of Serbia to use anything but the Ekavian dialect, and that is perfectly clear to anyone in Serbia. Now, what confuses you now is the confusion that I had then, and then it is on the basis of this confusion that you issue false indictments. If you look at the stamp, you will see that it is an institution that doesn't exist. The stamp testifies to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you talk about your confusion then, does that mean that you did not deliberately mislead your audience and that you also thought the document was genuine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I knew it wasn't authentic, but that's the method that was customary then in political conflicts in Serbia. The Democratic Party did something very similar to me. They Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. found my signature on one document, they attached it to another one by way of a photocopy, and then they pretended that it was my document. Perhaps it may seem strange to you, but that was the usual thing in our political life then. And I know what Mr. Nice has in store for us. Probably he's got something written up here that he likes and then we are going to see what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How did you actually get the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who knows how the document was made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question is how did you get it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, probably somebody in the party made it. How should I know? That was 12 years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Somebody in your party forged a document by Simatovic, you presented it as genuine to your party members, and then you reinforced the falsity by actually putting it in the magazine. That's how you treat your party members, is it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All the time or just sometimes?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm engaged in a propaganda war here, and you're the one who is lying, Mr. Nice, but I'm indicating two facts to you which clearly show that the document cannot be an original document. And had somebody brought criminal charges against me then, those two facts would be evidence in a court of law that this could not have been an original document. It cannot say "dodjeljuje" or "uspjehe". It can only be "dodeljuje" and "uspehe" in the Ekavian. So now you're asking me to remember all the details, and we thought we were just being politically clever at that time, 12 years ago. And now you want me to come up with all the details, yeah, we sat down and then we started carving all this up and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It comes ill from you, Mr. Seselj, to try to brand the Prosecutor as a liar having just, as a complete generalisation, accused everyone involved in politics at that time in Serbia of misleading the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to have to come back to this document because there is more material about Vakic that I want to deal with, but the accused -- the witness seems to think that in some way I am controlling the screen. I am not able to control the screen, but if the technical booth would give us the bit right at the top of the document so that -- or if the usher -- Mr. Nort can deal with that, then he can just read the bit at the top that's worrying him. No. That seems to be the wrong way. How about the other way? There we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, this is the bit at the top that you wanted -- that you thought somebody was keeping from you. Just read the bit at the top before we forget the point.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it says here is "Special Unit for Special Purposes of the MUP of Serbia." First of all, it is impossible for it to say "Namjene" in an official document of the Republic of Serbia. It has to be Ekavian. So there is no such unit either. It is obvious that this is not an official document. It would say "Special Unit for Special Purposes of the State Security Service of Serbia." Before that, it would say, "The Ministry of the Interior of Serbia." The document itself shows that it is a mockery. I don't know what else to call it. It's something totally lacking in seriousness. It's supposed to enrage people. Look, Ijekavian is not used officially in Serbia. Not a single authority in Serbia uses Ijekavian. So that's why the document was written this way, in order to generate confusion and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, we'll come back to Ekavian-Ijekavian later, probably tomorrow, we'll come back to this document later today, and I have a couple of other documents I want us to look at, but let's go back to the present exhibit, the 11th of November statement. The Court has already read ahead a little bit, but for the sake of the record I must now move on to the next sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I get a photocopy of this document that was on the ELMO a few moments ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It will be down in a couple of minutes if -- it's down now. It's provided now. It's not marked yet, so I'll deal with it probably after the break in more detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right, let's go back to where we were. If the usher would be so good as to make sure we're back to the previous document at page 5 of 16, as we're taking time, and we'll read on. So page up or camera down, whichever it is. "He is presently the head --" further down, please. "He is presently the head of the Serbian State Security Service Intelligence Administration. That is the original document. We also have a number of other documents out of which we have presented only several here. This is meant for you to see that our volunteers went to fight completely officially, that they were assigned with weapons --" it says they, but "^ sic weapons, ammunition and other military equipment in a regular way and that they also returned it in a regular way. For example, here is the proof that the Ministry of Interior Special Purposes Unit received war booty from our volunteers near Skelani," and there is a list of what they got: One, probably mortar, and another of 82 millimetres, a certain number of bullets, number of other types of weapons. You can see this one as well after the press conference. There is a stamp of the Special Purposes Unit on it. There are also receipts for the weapons of the volunteers who returned from the front. All of this proves that the Serbian Radical Party volunteers cannot be in any way accused of belonging to any paramilitary organisation. Their commanders in battlefields, their chief commanders were Obrad Stojanovic near Skelani, while in other battlefields, in Eastern Slavonia, for example, it was Mihalj Kertes, one of the main commanders of the Red Berets who are now trying to establish a reign of terror in Eastern Slavonia and who are trying to hide the evidence of serious crimes committed by some corrupt individuals from the regime lines, such as Goran Hadzic." Just pause there then. Is this truth or fiction in this last passage we read?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, you've got a mistake in here. It's Obrad Stevanovic. To the best of my knowledge he was a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And he was a witness here. We've seen him. Yes. And he was, was he not, indeed, and that man, who was a witness here, Obrad Stojanovic, it's the top of page 6 and it's the third line, I meant to correct it and I was looking for the original to be sure of it, that man acted as a commander-in-chief, whatever he may have said here, at the lines, didn't he? Not as a commander-in-chief, as a commander.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, he was a volunteer there, and he commanded some unit as a volunteer. Like others, Frenki was a volunteer, Badza was a volunteer, and now I put Mihalj Kertes in on purpose, although he was never at the front line, or actually he never participated in the war. But I'm trying to create confusion there on purpose. To the best of my knowledge, Obrad Stevanovic did spend some time there for a while as a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the effect of confusing your audience? What are they going to go away and do apart from scratch their heads?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, many people were scratching their heads, Mr. Nice, but you see, even unwillingly, 12 years later, I've caused a good effect. You believed this, and you issued an indictment on that basis, and you see it falling down now as if it were made of cards. You cannot base an indictment on hearsay. I'm just giving the names of all sorts of political officials whose names I knew at the time. I didn't mention others because I didn't know their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please stop. The question I asked you was what was -- what was your audience going to gain from this. I asked it in slightly different words, but it was clear. What was the purpose of lying to your audience in this way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question you asked was actually, and I think a more pointed one, what was the purpose of confusing the audience?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes. I'm grateful to Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was the purpose of confusing your audience?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My purpose is to present the participation of some policemen as volunteers in the war as their institutional participation in order to deliver a blow to Mr. Milosevic at the time when he was being highly cooperative with the Western powers in seeking peaceful solutions that I considered to be wrong for the Serbian people. That's the point. On the other hand, I attacked them because they are arresting my volunteers left, right, and centre. They're also breaking up my party, again on the basis of some kind of false documents and false arguments and God knows what kind of forgeries they used against us. We are striking back using the same methods. Perhaps ours were much milder than what they did to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very subtle stuff, isn't it, if I may suggest on the basis your answers being accurate, very subtle stuff because on this passage you haven't mentioned the accused directly at all, have you? You've gone for all sorts of other people; Frenki and Stevanovic and Kertes. Or is the reality this, that what you said here was true, as it has been in so many of these passages of your books that we've looked at where they damn as culpable this accused and the apparatus he controlled?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This cannot accuse Mr. Milosevic, because I was engaged in a propaganda war, and you got evidence today that this was indeed a propaganda war, and that in that propaganda war I resorted to the methods explained. You got the evidence today, and you don't want to show it to the Trial Chamber. Let's look at that too. What was my objective? To publish everything I ever stated with many contradictions. One day I thought historians are going to study all of this, and on the basis of that they're going to understand all the things that were going on. But now you want to look at all these volumes and volumes of mine, and over 50 have been published so far. You'd just like to extract what --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If it be the case that Obrad Stevanovic before this Court denied ever being in Bosnia, for example, that would be wrong, wouldn't it? As a volunteer or in any other capacity. If that's what he did, that would be quite wrong, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then it's incorrect, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I never saw him anywhere, either in Bosnia or in Krajina. But he was a high-ranking police official that I knew of, and it was convenient for me to attack him then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You can't have it every way. If you look at that sentence, "Their commanders in battlefields were Obrad Stojanovic near Skelani ..." The first part of the answer is yes, he was there. He was -- as a volunteer. Your second answer is that if he denied it, that would be wrong, and you're now trying to build a defence for him. When you said he was there as a commander, you were telling something that you knew to be true, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I am not trying to defend him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's move on to something else. At the bottom of page 6 of 16 in the English, and for you it will be towards the middle or bottom, probably, of page 291, you do turn to the accused, Mr. Milosevic. Let's see what you say about him. Bit further down. Thank you very much. You say this: "However, the Serbian Radical Party has bitterly fought the whole year long against the criminal state-financial Mafia that is in power in Serbia and in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. We have been gradually unmasking that Mafia, beginning from the Minister scandal, all the way to the General scandal. We've been unmasking all of them and now the time has come to unmask the main criminal named Slobodan Milosevic. Nothing in this country can be stolen on such a high level without his permission and his knowledge." Well, what did you mean about all that? We'll just pause. We'll read the rest in a second, but what did you mean by all that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see that I am attacking Mr. Milosevic as fiercely as possible, ruthlessly, to the very end. All the affairs that happened in Serbia over those years, I ascribe to him. For example, the ministers affair is the one that he personally unmasked. Our role was an unimportant one. The affair with the general is the one with Zivota Panic, is one that I personally unmasked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... from you, shall we, of life at the time. You -- earlier on in this article you explain the way you were attacked, and in the other article I think the way you were nearly killed and so on by organs of the state. It certainly was a case of a police state at this time, wasn't it? People could attack politicians in the way that you've described. Not a lot of point in describing it in any other way, is it? It was a police state.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a police state. The accident was an accident. Had they wanted to kill me, they would have killed me or I would have been seriously wounded. It seemed that the car in front of us skidded, we hit into that car, and I just hit my head on the roof, and it was a very small wound with very little bleeding, and again this was a good opportunity for me to attack Mr. Milosevic and his government for that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And all the other attacks that were mounted on you at the time to which this whole speech was a rebuff or a correction, all these other attacks, forged documents and all sorts of other things about Petkovic, you wouldn't say these were the actions of a criminally police state, would you, or would you?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was not a criminally police state. You see, the behaviour of the secret police in our political life is a legacy of the past from the old communist regime. There was an inertia involved. It's a fact that the police did deal with the opposition parties. The police had their own people in all opposition political parties, and they were gathering information about activities, about the leadership, et cetera. They did the same thing in the Serb Radical Party too. But we managed to unmask their main people in our party leadership, and we managed to throw them out of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The description of activities of the police in respect of opposition parties I must suggest to you is the clearest acknowledgement that this was indeed a police state. And when we come and look at the passage we've just been looking at, we see you describe it as being, in addition to that, a Mafia state, a crime-based state. Was that true?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the FBI in America also tries to infiltrate different organisations by sending in people of their own, even the trade unions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Further on --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- please listen to the question. Please listen to the question. When we look at the passage we've come across, you describe it as a crime-based state, as a Mafia state. Was that true?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Mafia started appearing over those years, that's true, and what I'm trying to do here is to portray all these bad things, including the Mafia activities, as being organised by Mr. Milosevic. It is true that the Mafia activity was felt there, but my propaganda trick lies in the fact that I tried to ascribe all of this for Mr. Milosevic, and I accuse him of everything that is negative; that which is truly negative, that I'm exaggerating, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If he wasn't responsible for all the criminal activity of the Mafia state, for what part of it was he responsible?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, he cannot be personally responsible for anything because he did not have any of this within the scope of his authority, but it is a fact that within the Socialist Party of Serbia there were people who were engaged in Mafia criminal activity, and the Mafia that rose during his years in power ultimately carried out a coup d'etat against Mr. Milosevic. That's a fact too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the end of this passage. "What could Jezdimir Vasiljevic, or Dafina Milanovic steal from Serbia? How could they succeed in robbing the people and the state without the consent of Slobodan Milosevic and without his support? The question is: Where is that money, the money that was stolen from people, from old foreign exchange savings, from the Loan for the Recovery of Serbia, the Loan for the Economic Recovery of Serbia, from all the privately owned banks, especially where is the money, the foreign currency obtained through the speculations with the primary issue of money. It's gone to Cyprus and to other banks." You're here describing a movement of money of which we've heard in evidence, you see, Mr. Seselj, and you're ascribing it to the accused, and he was responsible, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the negative things that were going on, both in actual fact and that that was simply fabricated, is what I ascribed to Mr. Milosevic. Your investigators kept looking for his alleged money in Cyprus and all over, and they found nothing. What I'm saying here is what all the pro-Western media in Serbia wrote about, all the pro-Western parties. These were standard accusations again the Milosevic regime over several years.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... so much in this document that may help us, but I have only a limited time. If the Chamber would go, please, to page 9 in the English, and in -- I'm afraid this hasn't been marked but perhaps you'll find it. It's to do with Arkan, and it's at the top of page 9 in the English. You should be able to find it by reference to BBC. I think it's probably part way down page 292 for you. And it says this: "For example, Radovan Stojicic, also known as Badza, with his members of the unit for special purposes took over the silo in Brdasin. Several hours after that, Arkan dashed in with his men, they recorded everything with video cameras, staged a fight, and it looked like they had done it. There were more examples. The worst thing is that the MUP units and Raznjatovic's Serbian Volunteer Guard collected the booty in tow-trucks. The war booty was collected with tow-trucks and resold here in Serbia. Besides, how come Arkan has a jeweller's shop in the city centre?" Just very briefly, is it right that Arkan was in a position to and did bring booty back in the form of war booty to Belgrade and sold it and made himself rich on it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Arkan was capable of doing that, but I am trying to directly link him up with the police here, expecting to hurt Mr. Milosevic in that way as well. To my knowledge, that was correct. Badza, as a volunteer, headed a unit of members of the Territorial Defence and took this very important silo in Brdasin that was a combat position. Several hours later - I was not an eyewitness but to the best of my knowledge - Arkan dashed in, pretended that there had been fighting, and then he liked showing this video footage in Belgrade later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next passage, please. Page 10 in the English, and for you the page where you start off, I think, with an answer that says, "Regarding Milosevic himself --" it's probably on 293, I think, and you say: "Regarding Milosevic himself, we do not have any documents. But we do have documents about his closest associates. For example, about the high officials in the Serbian Ministry of the Interior, we have documents regarding the Deputy Minister Stojicic, Badza, we have documents in connection with the head of the State Security Intelligence Administration Simatovic, Frenki. These documents are here, I have just presented them to you. His signature! There is also Mr. Vakic, who fought under the command of the high officials from the Serbian State Security Service. Documents cannot be found in relation to everybody, but they can be found for many ..." Asked "How much will that influence the image of Serbia?" You said: "Slobodan Milosevic, in the first place, harms the image of Serbia in the world." I think it's harms, it's crossed -- I think it is. "The most important for him is to preserve the one-party power in Serbia, that is the power of his own party, not caring about what troubles people may have to go through because of that." Is that true, all of that last passage?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that I did attack Mr. Milosevic in this way. As for the events that befell Serbia that time, in order to interpret that you would have to engage in scholarly work, and I used everything I could to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. attack Mr. Milosevic at that time. You have presented here just a very small portion of everything I said about him at conferences, at rallies, et cetera. I was engaged in a campaign against Mr. Milosevic at that time which was unseen in the Balkans before that professionally, according to a methodology that had been elaborated by Foreign Institutes for Special Warfare. Nobody did it better than I did, let me tell you that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. But it's quite true that you show your approach to Milosevic, and the question is whether in fact you showed it in full here or whether there was any margin reflected by the dishonesty or the propaganda. Would you turn over, please, in the English to page 11, and I think in the Serbian it will be to page 294, I think, and we can see how it is that you actually in this speech gave an attack on him. You say here: "Slobodan Milosevic led an honest and patriotic policy last year. If you remember, we revealed some scandals last year, but throughout the whole current year, we have been revealing many scandals involving Milosevic. The whole summer we struggled with him concerning the replacement of the generals --" there's a bit that's difficult for us to read in the English, don't worry about that. "The Supreme Defence Council has not adopted the state committee's report because Zivota Panic somehow has a hold --" I'm going too fast, I think -- "has a hold over Milosevic. Simply, they were sharing the booty. In Vukovar only, Zivota Panic confiscated $7 million of foreign currency. Nobody knows where the money has disappeared." And then you said this: "Milosevic acted as a patriot last year. He helped the Serbs in the Serbian Krajina. This year, however, he started leading defeatist policy and we have been working on unmasking that policy. He first accepted the Vance-Owen Plan and then he enabled people from his own party, especially Radmilo Bogdanovic, the League of Communists - Movement for Yugoslavia, where his woman rules the roost, and the Yugoslav Army Security Service to plot in the Serbian Krajina." Now, there's a description of your political view including your view of the accused's wife. Aren't you there actually stating your position about this accused in a way that didn't need you to make up documents or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did indeed set out my then standpoint about Mr. Milosevic, but some things are exaggerated. I told you what happened to the money from Vukovar. I continue to assert that the money from the Vukovar bank was taken away by Aleksandar Vasiljevic and that it disappeared. However, I'm attacking Zivota Panic here because he was the commander of the military district, and it was under his command that the forces were in Eastern Slavonia. But the person who actually stole the money was Aleksandar Vasiljevic. Whether it was precisely 7 million marks or dollars I don't know, but several million marks or dollars were taken away by Aleksandar Vasiljevic and that is a fact. Furthermore, I say here that the basic conflict started when Milosevic had adopted the Vance-Owen Plan. Then I attack his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, you attack his wife. Just a minute. You're allowed, of course, to say things which constitute attacks on other people. Having accused Panic of taking 7 million marks, you now want to say that it's the former witness here who gave evidence adverse to the accused, Aleksandar Vasiljevic. Can you please just point to the piece of evidence that enables you to make that accusation since you make it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I know. I have no material evidence but I said that publicly in Serbia before my arrival in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, we know that you say things for propaganda purposes that are wholly untrue. Now, you've said this about Aleksandar Vasiljevic. Can you point us, please, to a single piece of evidence to sustain that very serious allegation.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you several facts. The first fact is that this money was in the Vukovar bank. And what sort of evidence are you look for, Mr. Nice, documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You tell us then what the evidence is that shows it was Mr. Vasiljevic -- General Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The money was in the Vukovar bank, that's a fact, when Vukovar fell. This money was confiscated by the JNA. This money was taken away from Vukovar by General Aleksandar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ask the commander of the 1st Guards Brigade, for example, who took the money away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This money, according to the legislation in force, had to be handed over to the so-called military service of the National Bank of Yugoslavia, because all money acquired by the army in any way had to be handed over to the military service of the National Bank, whether it was war booty or some other kind of income or revenue. Whatever money came to the army had to go through that service. The bank -- the military was not allowed to have any revenue apart from the revenue paid through that service of the National Bank. However, I assert that this money was never handed over to that service of the National Bank and yet it was taken away from Vukovar by Aleksandar Vasiljevic. I stated that in public in Serbia before my arrival in The Hague. It's easy to attack Zivota Panic now that he's dead. Why he didn't initiate proceedings against Aleksandar Vasiljevic for the theft of the money, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you made the allegation against Mr. Panic when he was alive.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What action did he take?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that year, I attacked Zivota Panic because of a large scale financial affair in Belgrade, because he made it possible for his son and his son's private firm, Kentaur, to be one of the chief suppliers of the army. I raised the issue in the Federal Assembly, I started a campaign in the press, in the media, and because of that campaign Zivota Panic had to be replaced. There was a commission headed by the minister of defence, Pavle Bulatovic, and I handed over the documents I had to that commission. I did have papers to prove that. That's why the title of the book is The Chief of the General Staff on His Knees. I was proved to be right and soon afterwards General Panic was dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think it's an answer to the question but I'm going to press on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Last question on this document which, let me make it clear, I may be asking as with other documents to be accepted as true in parts where you say things adverse to the accused, can we go to page 14 in the English for your then stated perception of the way things operated in government. This is on page 296, I think, in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What page is that in Serb?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think it's 296. And there are a number of passages that I want to summarise really. In particular, towards the bottom of page 14 on the English, about a third of the way up, which I'll try and find for you if I can, you say this of Cosic. You say in a sentence that begins: "But that option didn't suit us. Cosic, being Milosevic's instrument, was much bigger a danger for us than Milosevic himself, because Cosic still had influence in the international public." Can you find that sentence?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then it reads on: "The fight with Milosevic, regarding the replacement of these generals, lasted the whole summer. Milosevic had to give in. He did it very reluctantly, but he did replace those generals together with a number of other honourable and capable officers. We announced in June that we would overthrow the Sainovic government, and we gave him a three-month period to show whether his government was capable of changing anything to the better in Serbia. Since it turned out that it wasn't able, we openly started overthrowing the government. The most difficult thing for Milosevic was that we unmasked his role in the Banja Luka issue. If we say that the Socialist Party of Serbia took part in it, as well as Radmilo Bogdanovic, who is the power behind the thrown of the regime in Serbia, if we say that the League of Communists - Movement for Yugoslavia took part in it, and if we say that the Yugoslav Army Security Service took part in it, then we should only have drawn the picture of Slobodan Milosevic on that big board in the Assembly ..." Now, just a couple of things. Is it right, as you say here of Cosic, that he was Milosevic's instrument?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, this is a political assessment. It's hard to say whether he was an instrument or not. The facts are that with the fall of Milan Panic, Cosic was weakened considerably. And at one point he adhered to the will of the ruling party. He tried to nominate the judges of the constitutional court on his own, but this did not get through the Assembly. And then he adopted the nominees of the Socialist Party, and they were elected. We, as the second strongest political party, were a little afraid of a sudden cooperation between Dobrica Cosic and Milosevic's party. We made use of a situation in which the pro-Western parties in the Assembly instituted a motion to topple Panic. So we decided that either we would replace Cosic or the republican government would fall. That's how we forced the socialists to accept the replacement of -- we had initiated that much earlier. I cannot say whether Cosic was an instrument or not. My assessment, my political assessment from that time was that he was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was the Banja Luka issue that's referred to on the foot of 14 in the English?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you the facts that were in existence. Based on those facts, I made accusations. The facts were as follows: Part of the soldiers of the army of Republika Srpska rebelled in Banja Luka against the central government of Radovan Karadzic, and they blocked Banja Luka for several days. The situation was very difficult. In the Federal Assembly, bearing in mind the bad relations between Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Karadzic, I attacked various government structures from Serbia, saying that they supported the coup d'etat perpetrators. This was a construction. However, it is true that there was an attempted coup d'etat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And just before I move from this document, although I will come back to Vakic, before I move from this document, is the position that the accused used you to do his dirty business for him sometimes when he wanted things achieved, pressure put on the government of that kind?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Never could Mr. Milosevic force me to do anything. Never could he make me do anything, and never did I do any dirty business for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could this be exhibited, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And as to the document that's been placed on the overhead projector --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's just get the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 894.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I will return to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about the certificate?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I return to that article after the break because that and one other document we may have to look at. Can we now distribute the next document, which is, for the interpreters, number 31 and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you understand, don't you, Mr. Seselj, that included in my and the Prosecution's allegations against you so far as material to this indictment, not your own, are the facts that you were a propagandist spreading hate of the kind that could lead to the commission of the most serious offences really known to man. You've understood that allegation, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This allegation is false. I understand that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the second thing is that you were allowed by the regime, of which this accused was in control, to spread the messages you spread or, to use your terminology, he actually instrumentalised you because it served his own interests. You understand that allegation, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. That is not true. That regime never instrumentalised me. Anything I said I spoke on my own behalf and on behalf of the Serb Radical Party of which I was the head. No one ever gave me permission to say things or prohibit me from saying other things. At that time, there was no possibility for anyone either to make me say something or stop me saying something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, is it possible that the regime might have used you, instrumentalised you without your being aware of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That's impossible too. Everything I said fitted into my own ideological concept which I advocated for many, many years before Mr. Milosevic came to power in Serbia, and for this reason I was systematically persecuted by the former communist regime. My books were banned, I was imprisoned, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To make it quite clear, Mr. Seselj, in case I haven't made it clear before, the Prosecution's position vis-a-vis you is that you were a lethally dangerous weapon that was allowed to operate in the territory of the former Yugoslavia by this accused, generating ethnic hatred. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never disseminated ethnic hatred. Whenever there were discussions of inter-ethnic relations, I only set out the truth, the historical truth and the current truth about contemporary events.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This document we're looking at is headed "I Accuse Milosevic." It comes from November the 12th, 1993. And if the Chamber would be good enough to go to page 12 in the English, and if you would go to the last page, I think, page 85 in the Serbian. You find a question that begins: "You think you didn't incite crime?" Do you find that question at the top of the page? It may be on the previous page. It's possible that it's on the previous page. "You think you didn't incite crime?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who is asking that? It's rhetorical or --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's an interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: An interview, oh.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You still haven't told me where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's on page 83 or 84 and it's from the question from the interviewer, "You think you didn't incite crime?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Page 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 12 for us, page 83 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: At the bottom of page 12 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you find it, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be that we haven't copied that page, and if so, that would be entirely my responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm just going to read you a passage. See if you can find this. There is a question you were asked by journalists, "You think you didn't incite crime?" and you say, "I never incited crime." You were then asked a question: "How did you then think your idea could come true, division with Italy on the borderline Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica?" When you find that question, please --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it here, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It would appear to be some shortcoming in the matching. I don't quite understand why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's also odd that you should think it's on the last page of the Serbian whereas it's far from at the end of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My apologies for the fact that the B/C/S wasn't available the first time, caused by my discovering another passage I wanted to read and not appreciating that it hadn't been presented in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You have the passage before you now that begins in the English at the foot of page 12 with the question in the Serbian, "You think you didn't incite crime?" You answered the interviewer, "No, I never incited crime." You then went on. The interviewer asked you: "How did you then think your idea could come true - division with Italy on the borderline Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica?" And you said this: "Maybe I did incite war. Not even that, I thought, I was convinced and I am convinced today that had there been no betrayal at the army top, had we had a free state leadership, we would have finished it in one stroke without the war. Had the army immediately withdrawn from Slovenia when I requested in a rally on Trg Republike Square to withdraw from Croatia to the Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica line, everything would have finished straight away. There would have been no war." That was your position then. I suppose --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would have been a good thing if your interpreter had this text in Serbian, because the interpreters are translating from the English and it doesn't fully correspond.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is there a material difference, before we take time on this?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no material difference, but it's not faithful to the original, if you care about that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next question is, and you can read from the Serbian original the answers. I'll read the question, you read the answer. Question: "You spoke a lot against the people of other ethnicities and of dismissing and persecuting such people." Your answer was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Prosecutor is asking you the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could you read --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Well, that's not a war crime." That was my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next question was: "But your intonation could have incited many people to commit war crimes." And your answer, please read it in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: "No. It could have incited people to hate."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you were engaging in activity that could have incited members -- sorry, citizens of the former Yugoslavia to hate one another, yes?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You have misinterpreted the previous question. The journalist says, "You have spoken a lot against people of other ethnicities and dismissals and persecution of those people." My response was, "That's not a war crime." But here the journalist is referring to specific persons. I attacked a group of people by name. These people were in Belgrade, although they were of other ethnicities, mostly Croats, and they participated in the propaganda war against the Serbian people. This was a group of journalists, and I enumerated them by name, and they were not only Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next question was: "It's a thin line between hatred and crime," to which you replied?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I hate many people but I haven't tried to kill them for that reason."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked, "Because you might not have been in such a situation - had you been in combat --" I don't think I need go beyond that. Well, no, we'll just finish these two questions. "Had you been in combat and someone stood before you unarmed..." you answered?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a mistake here. As this is a newspaper interview, it says here: "I was in the war, and I interrogated prisoners of war," but it must have been "talked to prisoners of war" or "interviewed them." I did have conversations with prisoners of war once or twice. I say in the prison in Knin or in Borovo Selo, for instance. I visited the prison in Knin in November 1991. There were Croat prisoners there and also arrested Serbs. I visited both groups. I spoke to them. Those people are still alive, and they can testify to the fact that I did not say a bad word to anyone. I asked them how they were being treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The journalist said, "There's no document that Hitler ordered to kill Jews, either." And to that you replied at the top of our page 14, please read the answer.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say there were orders, and that's correct. And I go on to add: "Although perhaps orally, according to witness testimonies. There were specific consequences and the person in authority had to be held responsible. I was never in authority in any state."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "You were close to the authorities," you were asked, "you can't deny that." And you said, "What does it mean to be close to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. authorities?" And you were asked, "It means to be an influential person," and you gave an answer, "How did that influence manifest itself?" The reality is, Mr. Seselj -- it's only the first part I want to ask you about on this document. The reality is you were giving hate speeches and they were an instrument to get or led to people committing these crimes as it happened in the interest of this accused. Did you not appreciate that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I deny that categorically. First of all, I did not hold hate-filled speeches. If I did say something in hate-speak, it was against particular individuals or groups, not people in the abstract. And these speeches were never meant to incite anyone to commit crimes. You have not a shred of evidence to prove that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... of this document. The first page in both English and Serbian, and the first long answer. Now, this is of course in your book, so you can see the format of it. If necessary, you can explain it. Having dealt with how you were arrested on the 20th of October, and the police had arrested many members of your party throughout Serbia, you were asked, "... is it time to present your evidence that you intend to use more tactics?" And you said this: "We have already presented some evidence. Several times I said we had no paramilitary formations, however what I didn't say is that our people waged war within the army units and Serbian MUP units on almost all battlefields --"

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where do you find this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First page. First page of the document in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the previous document. It's not the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, it's from the same book, and I'm hoping -- you've now got it. So good.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not the same book, it's not the same document. The previous was a continuation of five interviews, and this is a continuation of four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There must be some confusion here, because for us it's in the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that may explain why the pages don't seem to match. So something has to be done to put this in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I will check it at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But you give this answer: "We have already presented some evidence. Several times I said we had no paramilitary formations, however what I didn't say is that our people waged war within the army units and Serbian MUP units on almost all battlefields - on their own - never so far. And they were often under the command of Kertes, Stojicic, and Frenki, whose name I don't have here at the moment but he is head of intelligence in the Serbian SDB. Our volunteers cannot be accused of any crimes and those who were arrested aren't all members of the SRS," and so on. So here you're making it again quite clear that your units were on almost all battlefields under Kertes, Stojicic and Frenki. True or false.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a long interview I gave to the Nin journal I think in five installments, and I am repeating the same thing. You can see from the interview that there was systematic arrests of members of the Serb Radical Party, for the most part volunteers, and on my part I accuse and attack, and it's true that I did say that. But it's also true -- everything I said is true, that is about why I said that and in what context. The only way I could oppose this police action was to attack vehemently, to shoot between the eyes, because their accusations were false as well that the volunteers had committed crimes, looting, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May those parts be produced as an exhibit. May we arrange at the end of the session to ensure that the filed documents are a single pack in line with what the Judges have had?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 895.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, perhaps when you have done the review later, Mr. Nice, it may be better to have them as separate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Re-issue it. Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You gave us two documents. Are you about to go on to the other one? I mean, we have two separate things here. But everything you've asked about, so far as the English is concerned, is in one of them. So if this confusion is not sorted out here no doubt it will continue and generate three or four filings before it's sorted out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The original document before the Court had extracts from two chapters in English and one of those only in B/C/S. The additional document you had provided is the second translation in B/C/S, I hope. Can we, because there are a couple of outstanding issues --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, did you give it a number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 895, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The witness raised questions about the copy of Velika Srbija in which the certificate said to have been signed by Frenki was displayed. That, I think, is now available for distribution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is the document Judge Bonomy had referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't realise that's what Your Honour was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we very briefly, please, look at this because it's available for re-examination. If you'd look, please, at the article that surrounds the pictures of the document, in fact it's documents, there's more than one document, I haven't got time to go into them, said to have reflected service by your men. You see that the article, if we look at the English, the article as a whole, if you've got the article there in your magazine, is headed "The foundation of the Serbian Chetnik movement." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't received that article. What I have received is "The War Path of Branislav Vakic."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine. If we move over, please, I want to get a couple of extracts, you see a cross heading, page 3 of the English, "Baptism of Fire." Could you find that, please. That's on -- it's on page 63 -- no. I can't see the page numbers, I'm afraid. It's hard to see. But it's on the right-hand side of the second or third -- the right-hand side of the first sheet. Do you see that, "Baptism of Fire"?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then if you go to the first quotation of Branislav Vakic at the foot of our page 3, he says: "The volunteers travelled from Apatin to Nis on a regular bus route on the Nis-Ekspres. I set off in my own car with five of my fellow fighters. In Apatin we were welcomed by one of the Chetnik unit commanders, now the Chetnik Vojvoda Jova Ostojic. Under cover of darkness, we crossed the Danube in boats. The Ustasha boats patrolled the Danube. It was difficult and risky to cross the Danube at the time. The now deceased hero Vukasin Soskocanin waited for us on the other side." And so on. Is that part of Vakic's account published in your magazine correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that's right. He does tell of his experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Insofar as your magazine was publishing what Vakic was saying, was it publishing, as you understood it, a truthful account of his involvement in fighting outside Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, it's like this: This article was written, according to Vakic's account, by Nikola Dinic and Dragoljub Stamenkovic. I never read the article but I can read it now together with you, if you like, and then I can tell you where Vakic is right and where he is possibly not right, if there are such portions, but you must also bear in mind --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We don't have time for all that. I'm going to ask that the document be produced when I've looked at one more excerpt, and if you'd be good enough to turn over, it's about four sheets, I think, well, one, two -- on the fourth sheet you'll see a cross-heading saying "Eastern Bosnia." It's on the English page 14 and about -- probably in the Serbian text about ten or 15 lines down, this is recorded: "... I found out that Kuljanin was a communist and an officer of the state security service. Today, he is in the Vlasenica garrison command. Meanwhile, the 63rd Parachute Unit from Nis was deployed in Skelani." Is that accurate? In your magazine, you see.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Under the "Eastern Bosnia," sheet 4, right-hand side, underneath one of the documents signed in respect of service over -- in another country.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours find it at page 14, about ten lines up -- eight lines up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you can't find it --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tell me which paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Under "Eastern Bosnia." It's under the paragraph headed "Eastern Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it's halfway -- towards the end of that paragraph, actually, so it may be on the right-hand side column, and it refers to the 63rd -- yes, there we are, we can see it.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it says that, "Meanwhile, the 63rd Special Parachute Unit from Nis was deployed in Skelani." Is that true or false? It's in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is it true or false?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how these events evolved. This must have been 1993, after the seizure of a group of Muslims in a train in Strpci where the railway runs from Belgrade to Bar, and to the best of my knowledge, a unit of the police from Serbia on that occasion entered Republika Srpska and secured the eight kilometres so that there was not a repeat of what happened with this group of 20 Muslims who were taken off the train and killed in the surrounding parts of Visegrad. So that is one possibility. The other possibility is that this was at the time when the Muslim units from Srebrenica had broken through towards Skelani and started to attack Bajina Basta. However, I can't interpret now somebody else's article and what somebody else says.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, then, go to the end of the next paragraph, which I think you'll find is on the next page, and if the Chamber will go to page 15. He speaks at the end of this page about being frequently summoned for talks at the Serbian MUP special forces, personally meeting commander Obrad Stevanovic and his deputy Simatovic. Is that right? Were people like Vakic in regular contact with Stevanovic and Frenki?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: How should I know that if I wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this -- just a moment, please. Just a moment. I have some knowledge about this. Now, if we're talking about sending out this unit, the unit that secured the Belgrade-Bar railway line, then it entered the territory of Republika Srpska along with permission from the authorities of Republika Srpska. Then that could have been providing security for the eight kilometres of railway line, and it is a generally known fact that at that time a police unit from Serbia entered Republika Srpska because the Belgrade to Bar railway line which passes through Serbia and Montenegro throughout its length with its eight kilometres also passes through Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We may or may not have time to deal with that issue, I know you've raised it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the magazine that produces the document. There was a question about seeing the article as a whole. My proposition to the witness is going to be that what he said in his press conference about Vakic was accurate insofar as it dealt with deployment of Vakic outside Serbia. May this copy of the magazine be produced, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could it have a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 896.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And on the same or similar topic, may we look at another document, which is an extract from the Belgrade Telegraf, which we have the document itself, or a photocopy of the document itself, and we have an interview here between Miladinovic and Vakic. And although we can look, I think, on the first page, you see an answer by Vakic where he says: "These claims are serious." It's on our first page in English. "These claims are serious ..." Do you see that paragraph? It's the second paragraph in, I think, second column in. Yes?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in the second sentence of that, he says: "The late Vukasin Soskacanin invited us to Borovo Selo and there we got weapons, Thompson rifles from the then JNA --"

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "-- at the beginning of November 1991 --"

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "-- we, the Serbian Chetniks, were invited by the JNA and entered Vukovar via Negoslavci. At that time, we were given weapons by Veselin Sljivancanin, a major in the then JNA, and cooperated with it, that's the Yugoslav army." That's all true, what he was saying in this newspaper interview.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, I'd like to draw your attention to something that is very important. You claimed, referring to some of my statements against Mr. Milosevic, that in Borovo Selo we received weapons from the police, and here Vakic is confirming that those Thompsons, produced by Zastava, came to us from the JNA, from the Territorial Defence warehouse. He's not being quite precise there, in actual fact, but here is evidence going against your thesis a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next column for you, bottom of the column; next page for the Court, top of the page. Vakic says: "At the beginning of 1992, the JNA invited us to send our volunteers to the Krajina. I sent a large group of volunteers from this part of Serbia to JNA barracks in Bubanj Potok ..." True?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's at the -- on the first page, it's at the foot of the third column.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then we go to the next -- the same -- the same paragraph. He says: "During six months from January to July, more than 6.000 volunteers were stationed and trained in these Belgrade barracks and then sent to the region near Drnis, Divoselo, and Pocitelj." True? That's in Croatia, of course. True?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It cannot be correct. He's made a mistake here, because he says that in those six months from January to June 1992, whereas Divoselo and Pocitelj occurred in 1993 as far as my memory serves me. So he's mixed this up a bit, or perhaps the journalist in his interpretation did, because that's what often happens in newspaper interviews, that an abridgement is made by the journalist according to his own logic and then things like this happen. As far as I remember, Divoselo and Pocitelj happened in 1993, and that is not when they went from the barracks in Bubanj Potok.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Stay on the same page for the English, left-hand column, towards the top of the column there's an answer beginning, "At the beginning of 1993 ..." Halfway down that answer, we see this: "There were not enough weapons and uniforms for all of us. I sought help from Perisic, who was then commander of the 3rd Army, went to Skelani to meet him three times. He promised and supplied uniforms for fighters, underwear," and so on. That's true isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes. But look at what it says here. Just a minute, Mr. Nice. Don't skip over things. It says, "From Skelani I went to see him three times -" that is him, Perisic - "and he promised and really did supply me with uniforms for 80 fighters, underwear, some food, a set of night vision binoculars that I needed. I did not receive any weapons from him," it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We go on down to --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So an incomplete answer is always an incorrect answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next question and answer - I'm trying to get through this quite quickly - the next question leads to the answer from Vakic: "Even then, everything wasn't right. As early as 1992, our prominent volunteers, Zoran Doderovic and Milan Cuk, were killed by the JNA. Colonel Ljubisa Beara, Officer Vinko Pejcic and Major Ostojic were involved in that." And then the next part of the answer says: "By the way, Beara is the man who organised the famous 'September 1993' Banja Luka coup meaning to overthrow Karadzic." Now, two things: Beara is the man of course now indicted for Srebrenica, and the September 1993 Banja Luka coup is the incident for which you were blaming the accused in -- on the documents we've recently looked at. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look at this here. My accusation was on the basis of assumptions, constructions, and so on and so forth, whereas the Banja Luka putsch has not been elucidated yet and nobody has yet told us what happened there exactly. To the best of my knowledge, the SK Movement for Yugoslavia really was involved and up to 1993 it was a generals' party. There were most generals and officers of the former JNA forming that party and it forcibly took them into their ranks. Now, whether this is true or not is a question that remains unanswered. Ljubisa Beara was the head of the military service for security of the Main Staff of Republika Srpska. Quite obviously those services were involved in the Banja Luka putsch, but nobody ever elucidated and cleared matters up completely, and I made guesses, I construed matters, and it served my purpose at one point to attack certain people from Serbia, but I didn't attack Mr. Milosevic for a putsch and didn't accuse him of the putsch on that occasion. And you can find my speech from the Federal Assembly. I make no mention of him in that particular speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you -- sorry. Before you move on, going back to that last question, which -- previous one which Mr. Seselj elaborated on, I can understand why. I didn't understand it until I read it again, but you put a question that Perisic had promised and supplied weapons for 80 fighters. In fact, the document says uniforms and in fact he made the point that weapons were not supplied and it would be as well to check -- to correct the transcript on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we just move on then from where we were in the answers, although I'll come back to Beara and the accused in a second probably. The next question and answer ask if he mentioned cooperation with the MUP of Serbia, and Vakic said: "There's much cooperation. In battles from Skelani to Srebrenica, we fought alongside the special forces of the MUP, under the command of Obrad Stevanovic, the third man in the Serbian MUP. I had excellent cooperation from him on the Skelani battlefield. He had his headquarters in Bajina Basta, and I would travel from Skelani to talk to him. I would go to him whenever I needed something, and he would issue orders about where one should go. From the beginning of April until 25th of May last year, we fought alongside the special forces of the MUP." Then over the page in the English, it continues: "A little later, the MUP of Serbia invited us to prepare ourselves and, if need be, fight together with them. We responded to the invitation. I gathered the men and we went to a training centre on the Tara mountain during July and August last year. At that time, I was in contact with Frenki of the MUP special forces. The moment I gathered a sufficient number of volunteers, he would send an official MUP bus from Belgrade to Nis. From Nis my volunteers left for Tara to undergo training. At that time, I had about 400 people from Nis ... and from there Chetniks and volunteers with MUP special forces were supposed to set off towards Srebrenica or Gorazde if the Turkish converts launched a major offensive." Now, is all that, to your knowledge, true?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me to comment somebody else's text, but you must bear in mind that at the time in Serbia, and Vakic's cooperation with the MUP could have been realised just in two cases; in the case of protecting those eight kilometres of the Belgrade Bar railway line or at the time when the Muslim units attacked Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's not what it says, is it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the only possibility of him cooperating with the MUP units. Now, bear in mind one more thing. When you give an interview --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- for television --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if I may say, so please stop using volume. The suggestion that this is the only basis upon which his cooperation could have been realises is not borne out by the text, it wasn't borne out by what you said in the press conference, it wasn't borne out in the other document we looked at in your own magazine, I suspect. Now, what this account of Vakic is is exactly as you said in the press conference about the high level of cooperation. Is that because it's all true? And Stevanovic was indeed - Obrad Stevanovic, a witness here - was indeed a commander at the front?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all -- first of all, I'm telling you this now: Vakic followed the policy of hostility towards the Socialist Party of Serbia and the authorities of Serbia. Therefore, many of his statements here were overemphasised too, exaggerated. You don't want to hear the answer. You do not want to hear an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... didn't mention this before. You remember I said to you was Vakic there in the --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
