utterances.text: What, which?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you were giving the account of -- when we were asking you about your press conference which reveals that Vakic was the audience.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I tell you that Vakic wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You told us nothing whatsoever about his being with you in the business of misleading people.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are not giving me the opportunity of answering your questions at all. He was sitting at the press conference with me. He was there with me. And that's when I said those things that were discussed. And the interview dates back to that time. And his interview is within the frameworks of our settling of accounts with the authorities in Serbia. It falls under that heading. And there's no doubt there, if there was -- really was contact between him and Obrad Stevanovic, then it could have occurred only at the point when Obrad Stevanovic went to protect the part of the Belgrade-Bar railway line or when the Muslim attack on Bajina Basta was refuted. So those are the only two instances when this could have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any third case or instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could the newspaper article be produced, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 897.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I shall have to deal with matters much more briefly with documents to support. Sometimes I shall put things without documentary support and see what the witness says about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it right that your group in any sense liberated the area around Srebrenica, your men liberated the area around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, when the Muslims at the beginning of the year broke through into Serb villages around Srebrenica and when a large number of civilians was killed, then two groups of volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party went to help out the Serbs over there and the Serb army, and at that time I toured the front line around Srebrenica. That was at the beginning of 1993. I was at the funeral of the civilians who were killed, held in Skelani, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you ever expressed the view that Milan Martic may have sold himself out to Milosevic on the basis that Milosevic promised he'd nominate him as a candidate for the Presidency of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of 1993, when the Serbian Radical Party entered into a conflict with the Socialist Party of Serbia and Mr. Milosevic, Milan Martic, with a group of officials of Republika Srpska Krajina, issued publicly a statement in which he attacked the Serbian Radical Party and myself personally. And we then attacked Martic in the same way and to the same extent. So whether this was in response to the attack, that is not impossible. When Milan Martic was put forward as a candidate for the president of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, the Socialist Party of Serbia publicly supported his nomination or candidature. And I think that there were activists of the Socialist Party who went to Srpska Krajina to support him over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you describe Martic as Slobodan Milosevic's vassal?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not improbable. I might have said that to be insolent towards him and give him equal measure for the insults he hurled at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is that because it's true that these men or this man was the vassal, the puppet of this accused?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Milan Martic was not a vassal, and he was not a puppet of Mr. Milosevic. However, he was on better terms with Mr. Milosevic and the authorities in Serbia than Milan Babic was. And the authorities in Serbia were better disposed to Martic. They didn't like Babic. The authorities in Serbia didn't like Babic because they thought he was inconstructive, too radical, even extremist, and so on and so forth, those were the rumours circling about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In your account of what happened at Srebrenica, did you make it plain that you fought on many fronts with Frenki?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never met Frenki anywhere nor did I fight him anywhere, until I met him here in The Hague prison. Frenki was a volunteer in Srpska Krajina. That is where he led a unit which wore red berets on their heads, and part of the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party were sent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't understand the question, Mr. Nice, "... did you make it plain that you fought on many fronts with Frenki?" Now, is that as an ally or an enemy?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As an ally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the witness has misunderstood the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, the suggestion is that at some stage you may have acknowledged, may have said that you fought together with, alongside Simatovic in the area around Srebrenica. Did you say that? Was it true?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never said that. Find me where you say I said that, that we fought with Simatovic around Srebrenica. I never said that. However, in 1993, I could have attacked Simatovic for various things, in 1994 and 1995 as well, right up until that major conflict lasted. If Branislav Vakic really did have contacts with Obrad Stevanovic and Frenki with respect to Srebrenica, it could have been only in two instances, and I state that quite categorically.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can just distribute this. This comes from a book, "A Red Tyrant from Dedinje." That's a book of yours, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters have the tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry, yes. The tab number is 36. It may be -- we'll just see what the witness says about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It says 35 and 36.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 35 and 36, yes. But if you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The quotation that I have in mind is to be found in the papers given to you on the first sheet of text, I think. No, it's on page 100. If you see the page numbers in the bottom, left-hand corner. Go to an answer that heads -- is headed: "On his personal cooperation with the army and the police, Vojislav Seselj stated the following ..." Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "We cooperated on the issue of war in the Republic of Serbian Krajina and Republika Srpska. We received weapons from them. We received them from the army too," and so on. And then it goes on at the end: "Our men liberated the entire area around Srebrenica and they closed in on Srebrenica. Further, we also fought on many fronts with Frenki Simatovic ..." Now, it doesn't say in the -- in the way I've read it out there that he was with you in Srebrenica, so it may be that that needs some adjustment, but is it right that you fought on many fronts with Frenki Simatovic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, as long as the fighting was going on for Republika Srpska Krajina, the volunteers from the Serb Radical Party were there too. From that point of view, it can be considered to be correct, but you can see from here that I'm attacking the police as well. A realistic fact is that we got weapons from the army and now I'm twisting that and saying we got it from the police. Why would we be getting it from the police when everybody else got it from the army and all the volunteers were within the JNA? And thirdly, in 1991 the JNA could have mobilised the entire police of Serbia and sent them to the front line under the command of the then generals. That was in accordance with the then law and constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My suggestion to you, and I'm sure you'll understand it, is that there is no reason for this subterfuge where you're giving accounts of things like this and what you're saying is true, and you're trying to deny it now because you know the damage it's doing to this accused. That's the reality, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. I am not here to protect the accused. The accused brought me here as a Defence witness to testify truthfully about the facts, and it was his calculation that the facts would work in his favour. The fact is that long ago we did not really choose our weapons when fighting against the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The witness has denied the accuracy of this passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how fair it is to put this kind of question, because the atmosphere here has to do with Srebrenica and the question of 1995 has to do with Srebrenica. Obviously all the questions that are put to Mr. Seselj here have to do with 1993, not 1995. So I don't think that the questions should be that confusing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I don't find them confusing, I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, although I've been hoping to restrict the amount of material produced, he's given an answer to the effect that some of the things here he said were untrue, so maybe this document should be produced as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let it be produced.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 898.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And can we press on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I -- perhaps I'm missing something here, but the point the accused has made, this document was published in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the relief of Srebrenica that's being talked about there occurred when?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not 1995. Shall we move on to -- Your Honours, just give me one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Can we look, please, at this document, and for the interpreters, number 43. This comes from your book "The Witch from Tolstoj Street." The passage that we've had copied, and it's only a short passage, can be found on page 231 in your text. It's about a third of the way -- halfway down, thank you, where you say this of Arkan: "As for Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, he is the man of Slobodan Milosevic. By the mere fact that he is the man of Radmilo Bogdanovic and Radovan Stojicic, Badza, Milosevic --" full stop. "Milosevic cannot attack his own man. Why can't they try Arkan? Because they would then have to try Arkan's boss Badza. In this war, Arkan served as a cover-up for Badza. Arkan did nothing without the regime in Serbia being aware of it. To try Arkan means to try yourself. That is the position of Slobodan Milosevic." Well, those are your words in 1994. Are they true?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In 1994, I tried to link Arkan to Mr. Milosevic as much as possible in order to damage Mr. Milosevic politically as much as possible. I had no proof of that. Truth to tell, Arkan was on good terms with Badza and that was well known. However, I used that fact in order to trouble Mr. Milosevic politically. At that time, Arkan was so powerful that even the authorities didn't dare deal with him. He had great extra-institutional power; a lot of money, a criminal organisation, and so on. Even the authorities, the government, was afraid of clashing with Arkan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In the question "Why can't they try Arkan," who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "They" is the authorities. I already told you about the case when I talked to a police inspector who came to talk to me on account of my accusations to the effect that Arkan had killed a certain Eso Lero from Belgrade. That police inspector told me that they had a lot of indications but they could not present evidence against Arkan. They didn't dare take steps against him. Now, what happened. No one dared testify against Arkan, even people who had knowledge. He also had some people from the regime who he had bribed successfully and who protected him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your -- your observations here are quite clear that there's a reason he can't be tried and that's because it would uncover the connections between him and the top of the regime, which is a pretty serious allegation against the regime in any event.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a very serious accusation, just like all my accusations against Mr. Milosevic from that time, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you saying that Arkan was sort of above control? Did he run the war himself perhaps? Did he start the war? Did he answer to no one? What is your position on Arkan?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Arkan, when he joined the war, had double motives. On the one hand patriotic, because he was a brave man. And I think that he really did have certain patriotic inspirations. But in addition to that, Arkan's a criminal, the greatest criminal in Serbia, at that, and he could not curb that even in times of war. So his inclination towards crime became even more emphatic then. Arkan was really close to Badza. I told you during the first days of my testimony that Badza was killed on account of tobacco trafficking, and I told you who killed him, to my knowledge. So Badza was not averse to taking part into such things either, abusing his high office in the police. What is emphasised here and what cannot be proved is the link between them and Mr. Milosevic on the other hand from that point of view. What I am construing here is an attack against Mr. Milosevic by relying on some realistic facts that actually could support that. However, when you try to work out an indictment on that basis, you see that that is no basis for an indictment. This can be used in political battle, but when you try to deal with it in a court of law, you see it as untenable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd ask this document be produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Mr. Seselj, let me make it quite plain to you: My suggestion to you is that when you were saying that effectively Arkan was the accused man via Badza, you were simply revealing the truth, and you knew it, and you know it now.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look at another document.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you say that your whole purpose in this passage that we are looking at was to embarrass Mr. Milosevic by linking Arkan with him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That was the purpose of this interview, like of a series of other interviews that I gave over those several years. I personally am convinced that Mr. Milosevic never actually met Arkan. However, some people in the authorities were in cahoots with Arkan. That's a fact too. All of Arkan's power was outside the institutions but often based on bribing some people from the regime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And in relying on these and other documents with your speeches and interviews, you say the Prosecution has misdirected itself in that it has failed to distinguish between statements which you make for political purposes and statements which actually represent facts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. I insist on that, because everything that was said in the heated Serbian public political debate, said by me and other Serb politician, that cannot be taken for granted, and a serious indictment cannot be based on that. That is impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does that cast doubt on your evidence as a whole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, it is for you to judge. I am counting on the court of history. I'm convinced and I take as a point of departure the fact that this trial remains as a very significant trial in history irrespective of its outcome. What I care about is the judgement of history about my role, about my honesty, about my integrity, about my honour, et cetera. What your judgement is going to be is your own affair. Your judgements are also subject to public scrutiny.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I'm afraid the next exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We need a number for the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry, a number for the last one, I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 899.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, this sort of attack, you said these attacks are responses to the conspiracy of the government and arrest of your volunteers. Could you give us the number of volunteers who had been arrested at that time and how -- during how long period were they arrested at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot give you an exact number, but there were quite a few. Dozens, I would say. Srem, Backa, Sabac, within Serbia proper, et cetera. And they were kept in prison for about a month as a rule. They were all released. As far as I can remember, later on there were no trials against any one of them. All of this happened during the time of the election campaign, on the eve of the elections in 1993, when we wanted to overthrow Nikola Sainovic's government and Mr. Milosevic dissolved the national Assembly when he realised that the government would fall. The regime took repressive measures against us, and we responded in any way we could think of. Whatever crossed our mind we used as political ammunition against the regime. You know, that is a state of despair when at moments we even feel powerless, when we think that the regime will succeed in destroying our party, when among my closest associates I start feeling fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next exhibit I don't have in English but I'll deal with the exhibit tomorrow, but if, with the leave of the Court, we can just lay a paragraph with Mr. Nort's assistance, I will point out the bit I want - that bit - on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And this comes from your book "Serbian Spouses Ceausescu" published I think in 1994. Published in 1995, but I think the passage we're looking at is 1994, and if it can go on the overhead projector, please. Could you start reading at the -- the end of the first page. Just read it out to us nice and slowly, where you say: "I have prepared myself for The Hague, bypassing Milosevic." Do you see that passage?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can barely read this, and I don't really have it in front of me. It's not the right reference. You haven't given me the right reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] "... myself for The Hague, bypassing Milosevic. Can you imagine the following scene at The Hague trial?" Can you see that? Maybe further up the page?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still can't see that. I haven't got that in front of me, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters have the tab number as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's tab number 44.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just try that passage, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be this passage we want you to look at. Yes.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the beginning, Carl Druga [phoen] said -- can you read that for us, please, where it says, "I prepared myself for The Hague."

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Journalist's question is: "The foreign media have been writing that Slobodan Milosevic is preparing you for The Hague." That's the question. And I give the following answer to that question: "I have prepared for The Hague apart from Milosevic. Can you imagine the following scene at The Hague trial: I'm sitting in the dock, and I keep sitting -- and I keep a seat right next to me empty, reserving it for Milosevic." And then another rhetorical question, that's what follows: "How can Milosevic send me to The Hague without previously sending Radmilo Bogdanovic, Mihalj Kertes, Jovica Stanisic, Radovan Stojicic Badza, Franko Simatovic Frenki, and others?" This is an interview after I was released from prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is in 1994. What was it that connected in your mind this accused and Kertes, Badza, Frenki, and Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the key question is what was it that motivated certain foreign and -- journalists at home. Why was Milosevic preparing me for The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... because, you see, you've identified there what might be thought a number of people said to have been in a joint criminal enterprise, and you did it in 1994. Now, I wonder what it was in your mind that connected these people before indictments were issued. Tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was in my mind was that Slobodan Milosevic was preparing me for The Hague. First, I demonstrated that I was not afraid of The Hague, because after these speculations I made a telephone call to The Hague myself, and I'm sure that you have evidence that I called two or three times. Now, what is in my mind? You are not in a position to compel me to answer the way you want me to. I am retaliating here against Milosevic's attack, and this provokes laughter in the public, and I say off I go to The Hague and I'm keeping Mr. Milosevic a seat right next to me. And of course people laugh. And then I attack the key people in the police force. Radmilo Bogdanovic was minister of police in 1991. Mihalj Kertes was head of the federal SDB, Jovica Stanisic of Serbian SDB, Radovan Stojicic Badza the chief of the intelligence service within the SDB, then Franko Simatovic. I'm giving a list of all the top officials from the SDB at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we'll have to follow this up tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll produce the document with English translation.
